$comment: Scope: the external "brick" linear power supply, the mainboard RF modulator, and the mains side. Everything below each root is inline. Shared upstream ids are referenced by string. Note that 120407 is the PSU assembly number; 250407 is the C64 motherboard assembly number - they are not the same thing (see the note on c64.psu).

roots.name: Commodore 64 external 'brick' power supply
roots.description: A sealed black ABS box roughly 150 x 100 x 60 mm that sits under the C64 and converts wall mains into 5 V DC for the logic plus unfiltered ~9 V AC for the cassette motor, the RF modulator, the VIC-II's CAN +5 V rail, the SID's +12 V doubler and the 50/60 Hz time-of-day clock. It is a linear supply: an iron-core transformer, two rectifier diodes, one 4700 uF electrolytic, one three-terminal 5 V regulator and a folded aluminium heatsink, all buried under a minty-green epoxy pour from 1983 on.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz, 40-46 VA (North American 902503-02 / 251053-02 builds)

facts.label: 5 V DC output
facts.value: 7.5-8.5 W rated (1.5-1.7 A), unregulated 5 V AC rail separate

facts.label: 9 V AC output
facts.value: 6.7-9.0 VA, unfiltered sine, galvanically separate winding

facts.label: Output connector
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN (4-pin on some builds)

facts.label: Approvals seen on case
facts.value: UL 13J5 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER', CSA, NLS, 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN'

facts.label: Made in
facts.value: Singapore (251053-02); transformer marked 'MP' (Miles-Platts, UK)

roots.note: Part-number correction: the external supply is ASSY 120407; 250407 is the C64 *motherboard* (the version in this tree's spine file). Regulator silicon changed three times in three years: a discrete 2N3055/2N3792 pass transistor in the earliest 'repairable' silver-label boxes, a plain 7805-class three-pin regulator in the potted 1983-84 units, and a Sanken SI-3052P in the later 902503-02. Diodes are 400GI or 1N5400, not 1N4001, in most builds.

children.name: Mains transformer, 40-46 VA
children.description: The whole of the supply's energy conversion. One primary on 117 V mains, a centre-tapped ~18 V secondary feeding the 5 V regulator, and a separate ~9 V winding feeding straight out to the C64. The two secondaries are galvanically isolated from each other as well as from the primary - that isolation is what lets the C64 tie their grounds together only at the rectifier.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 40 VA (3-83 build) / 46 W (13-83 build) input at 117 V 60 Hz

facts.label: 9 V winding
facts.value: 9 V AC 9.0 VA, protected by a 3 A fuse in the conductor

facts.label: HV winding
facts.value: 18 V AC centre-tapped, pins 6/7/8 on 902503-02, protected by a 5 A (slow) fuse

facts.label: Maker's mark
facts.value: MP (Miles-Platts, Leicester, UK - bobbins and insulation systems)

children.note: The 'MP' mark on the core is most likely Miles-Platts (founded 1971, a UK bobbin and insulation specialist whose own company history lists inch-lamination and metric-lamination bobbins), i.e. the coil former and interwinding materials rather than necessarily the whole assembly.

children.name: E-I laminated silicon-steel core
children.description: A stack of punched E and I laminations with interleaved joints, taped along the yoke edges with a single wrap of masking or Kapton tape. For a 40 VA unit at 60 Hz the stack is maybe 25-35 mm tall in 0.35-0.5 mm plate, and it is clamped hard enough that the laminations must be isolated from each other by the oxide scale left on the punched edges.

facts.label: Lamination thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm or 0.5 mm electrical sheet (era range for small power transformers)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: grain-oriented electrical steel, silicon content ~2-3.5 wt%

facts.label: Lamination pitch
facts.value: roughly 20-30 mm; E and I interleaved in a 2:1 or 3:2 sequence

children.note: This brick is a laminated-steel design, not a ferrite design - the teardown shows a stack of discrete plates wrapped in tape at the yoke edges. Ferrite E/U cores were used in some later Commodore supplies (C64C, C16/Plus4 white brick) where they gave a smaller, lighter, lower-loss core at higher unit cost.

children.name: Punched E and I lamination
children.description: One E and one I punched from a strip of grain-oriented electrical steel by a high-speed progression press, roughly 200-600 strokes per minute. The die is a hardened tool-steel stamping die with a compound profile; the strip is fed on a roll and the interlamination burr left by the punch is small enough not to short adjacent plates.

facts.label: Press rate
facts.value: 200-600 strokes/min (high-speed progression press)

facts.label: Burr height
facts.value: ~10-25 um, sets the shorted-turn loss

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: the E is usually punched with the rolling direction across the yoke so flux runs along the grain

children.name: High-speed stamping press
children.description: A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.

children.name: Hardened tool-steel stamping die
children.description: Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.

children.name: Grain-oriented electrical steel (Hi-B)
children.description: Steel whose crystal grains are aligned so the easy magnetisation axis runs along the sheet. Magn permeability along the grain is several times higher than across it, so a transformer built from oriented steel needs roughly half the core cross-section of one built from hot-rolled plate. It is made by cold rolling to 0.35 mm, then annealing in a stream of hydrogen at 1100-1200 C, which lets the austenite grains rearrange into the aligned 'Goss' texture.

facts.label: Final thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm (Hi-B) or 0.5 mm

facts.label: Silicon
facts.value: 2.0-3.5 wt%, added to kill eddy currents and raise resistivity

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: <100> grain, ~1 mm domain size

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 A/m after the magnetic anneal

children.note: Oriented electrical steel is far too expensive for a 40 VA consumer transformer in 1982; a low-cost supply like this would normally use non-oriented or even hot-rolled mild plate. The Hi-B chain is given here because it is the canonical route to laminated core steel and because better Commodore supplies did use oriented stock - mark the specific material of this brick as unverified.

children.name: Cold rolling to 0.35 mm
children.description: A reversing four-high cold mill takes hot strip down through several annealing and rolling passes to 0.35 mm, with the rolling direction being the future flux direction. Reduction ratios above 20:1 in the final pass are what set the grain elongation.

children.name: Magnetic anneal in hydrogen
children.description: Coils of 0.35 mm strip are annealed for 20-40 hours at 1100-1200 C in a stream of high-purity hydrogen at dew points below -60 C. Hydrogen both removes oxygen that would pin grain boundaries and, on cooling through the Curie point at about 770 C in the field-free furnace, lets the austenite transform into oversized aligned grains.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 20-40 h per coil load

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: dry hydrogen, dew point below -60 C

facts.label: Field during cooling
facts.value: field-free (magnetic field anneal requires a field; the high-volume process is the field-free variant)

children.note: Strictly the two variants are 'grain-oriented' (field-free hydrogen anneal, the dominant 1980s process) and 'orientation by magnetic field' (applied field during the Curie-point cooling). The field-free hydrogen anneal is what Hi-B and most 1980s GOES plants ran.

children.name: High-purity hydrogen
children.description: Made in the 1980s by steam methane reforming of natural gas followed by pressure-swing adsorption and a cryogenic final purification to 99.999%. It was the standard controlled-atmosphere gas for grain-oriented electrical steel because it neither oxidises nor carburises the surface.

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: natural gas, steam-methane-reformed

children.name: Upstream: ore to hot-rolled sheet
children.description: The chain that makes the steel the laminations are punched from, from hematite ore through sinter, blast furnace, basic oxygen furnace, continuous casting, hot rolling, descaling and a primary base anneal, before the cold rolling and magnetic anneal that make it 'oriented'.

children.name: Iron ore concentrate, ~62-66% Fe
children.description: Run-of-mine hematite and magnetite is crushed and either shipped as lump ore to a blast furnace or upgraded to sinter/pellet. Commodore's steel chain in 1982 was almost entirely sinter-based: the ore was blended with coke and limestone, sintered on a Dwight-Stewart travelling grate into 5-6 cm porous sinter, and charged hot.

facts.label: Fe content
facts.value: 62-66 wt% for sinter feed

facts.label: Sinter basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 ratio ~1.0-1.6

children.name: Limestone flux
children.description: Calcite crushed to 3-6 mm and used both as sinter flux and as the blast-furnace flux that combines with silica to form a fluid slag. It is mined quarried and used essentially as dug.

children.name: Limestone quarrying and calcination
children.description: High-grade calcite is extracted by drilling and blasting, then crushed in two stages to 3-6 mm for the sinter mix and to 25-75 mm for the furnace burden. Only a small fraction is calcined; the bulk goes to the sinter mix as a flux, and the remainder goes down the furnace to become the fluid lime slag. Calcination itself, CaCO3 to CaO plus CO2, happens in the sinter mix and in the coke ovens.

facts.label: CaCO3 content
facts.value: >=52 wt% CaO equivalent for metallurgical limestone

facts.label: Decomposition
facts.value: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 above ~900 C

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: ~0.4-0.6 t limestone per tonne of hot metal

children.name: Metallurgical coke
children.description: Metallurgical coke is made in 1980s batteries or coke ovens by carbonising coking coal at 1000-1100 C in the absence of air; later plants added petroleum coke to the blend. It is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace.

children.name: Blast furnace and hot metal
children.description: A 300-1000 m3 shaft furnace charges sinter, coke and limestone in a burden; preheated blast at 900-1200 C burns coke to CO, and the burden descends against the ascending gas, being reduced from Fe2O3 through Fe3O4 to Fe. The furnace runs continuously for years, tapping iron at 1450-1550 C every few hours.

facts.label: Reducing gas
facts.value: CO/CO2, 20-25% CO at the tuffere

facts.label: Output
facts.value: ~1.5-2.0 t iron per tonne of sinter burden

children.name: Cowper stoves and the blast
children.description: The 900-1200 C blast is not heated directly: cleaned top gas from the furnace is burned in a refractory-lined Cowper stove, a tall cylindrical regenerator roughly 8-10 m across, and the 300-500 C exit gas is recovered in a gas-cleaning plant of cyclones and scrubbers. A furnace has three or four stoves, each on a 20-40 minute cycle.

facts.label: Blast temperature
facts.value: 900-1200 C at the tuffere

facts.label: Cowper cycle
facts.value: 20-40 min per stove, 3-4 stoves

facts.label: Blast volume
facts.value: 1000-2500 m3/min for a 1000 m3 furnace

children.name: Silica-alumina refractory brick
children.description: Stove and furnace linings are fired silica brick or aluminous firebrick, made from carefully graded silica sand or bauxite blended with a clay binder and fired in a tunnel kiln. Getting the grain size distribution right matters more than the chemistry: a graded pack gives a lining that survives thermal shock without spalling.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1400-1500 C in a tunnel kiln

facts.label: Refractoriness
facts.value: SiO2 94-98% for silica brick; Al2O3 40-50% for firebrick

children.name: Tapping the hot metal
children.description: Every three to four hours the drill is run through the tap hole and the hot metal runs into torpedo ladle cars holding 100-300 t. Skulls of solidified iron must be broken out afterwards with castings, which is why a blast furnace has a cast-house full of mud guns and running bars. The slag, lower in density, is skimmed off the top of the ladle.

children.name: Hot metal desulphurisation
children.description: Electrical-steel heats need sulphur below about 0.01% because sulphur embrittles steel. In the 1980s this was done either in the ladle with basic slag stirrer agitation or by injecting lime and aluminium powder with a lance under pressure of compressed air.

facts.label: Reagent
facts.value: CaO + Al powder, or soda ash, injected at ~4-8 bar

children.name: Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking
children.description: Hot metal is charged with scrap and lime into a tilting vessel and a water-cooled lance blows oxygen for 15-25 minutes. The carbon content is adjusted to whatever the rolling mill needs - around 0.05-0.1% for the electrical-steel grades - and the heat is tapped at about 1600 C.

facts.label: Target carbon
facts.value: 0.05-0.10 wt% for low-carbon electrical steel

children.name: Continuous cast slab and hot rolling
children.description: The molten steel is cast continuously into a 200-300 mm slab through a water-cooled mould with electromagnetic stirring, then hot rolled on a reversing mill straight down to 2-4 mm. The surface is descaled with high-pressure water or a mill scale breaker, and the strip is coiled.

facts.label: Descale
facts.value: HP water or reversing mill scale breaker

children.name: Base anneal
children.description: Hot-rolled low-carbon steel is coiled and annealed in a bell or stack furnace at 650-800 C, then pickled in dilute hydrochloric acid to remove mill scale and, if it is to become oriented steel, cold rolled and given the hydrogen magnetic anneal described above.

children.name: Core stack assembly and clamping
children.description: E and I plates are stacked in alternating layers with the joints staggered so no section of the stack has an unbroken air gap, then clamped end to end by angle plates and bolts or by rivets through the yoke. The joints are the dominant core loss, so the assembler has to keep the interleaving sequence right by hand.

facts.label: Interleave
facts.value: E-I-E-I, joints staggered by half a pitch per layer

facts.label: Clamp
facts.value: steel angle plates and M4 bolts, or pop rivets

children.name: Clamp bolts and angle plates
children.description: Mild steel angle plates bolted across the yokes, or two long tie bolts through the core legs, with the axial clamp force chosen so the interlaminar pressure is roughly 3-10 kg/mm2 - enough to stop the stack buzzing at 50 Hz, not so much that the punched edges crack.

children.name: MnZn ferrite E-core alternative
children.description: Later Commodore bricks and the C64C/Plus4 supplies switched to a pressed manganese-zinc ferrite core. Ferrite has much higher resistivity than silicon steel so it can be used as a solid moulded shape with no lamination joints, giving lower core loss at 60 Hz and a much lighter assembly - at several times the material cost, and with a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill.

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: ~10^5 ohm.m vs ~5x10^-7 ohm.m for silicon steel

facts.label: Saturation
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 T (much lower than steel, so the core must be bigger)

facts.label: Loss at 50-60 Hz
facts.value: 5-20 kW/m3 at 200 mT

children.note: Which Commodore supplies used ferrite and which used laminated steel varies by part number and I could not verify it per part number from primary sources. The 251053-02 teardown clearly shows laminated plates.

children.name: MnZn ferrite powder blend
children.description: A pre-mixed powder of iron oxide, manganese oxide and zinc oxide, ball-milled to a few microns. Zinc raises the resistivity and pushes the useful frequency band up; manganese lowers the magnetostriction and kills the 50 Hz mechanical buzz that would otherwise be audible inside the C64.

facts.label: Typical blend
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-60 mol%, MnO 5-15 mol%, ZnO 15-30 mol%

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 1-5 um after 24-48 h wet ball milling

children.name: Manganese ore and oxide
children.description: South African 'Highveld' or Gabon Gabon-type manganite is roasted and reduced to manganese oxide, then used as the fluxing component of the blend. Manganese is what gives MnZn its low magnetostriction.

children.name: Ore roasting
children.description: MnO2 ore is roasted in a fluid-bed or shaft furnace at 700-1000 C, driving off moisture and converting the higher oxides, then the product is leached or carbon-reduced.

children.name: Zinc concentrate
children.description: Sphalerite flotation concentrate from a zinc mine, roasted to zinc oxide then reduced in an Imperial Smelting furnace or electrolytically to zinc metal or zinc oxide. The oxide goes straight into the ferrite blend.

children.name: Iron oxide base
children.description: High-purity ferric oxide, made by roasting hematite ore or by precipitating iron hydroxide from pickling acid, is the majority component of the blend.

children.name: Dry pressing and sintering the E-core
children.description: The powder is mixed with 1-3% PVA or PVA/PVP binder plus a lubricant, granulated, uniaxially dry pressed in a steel die to the E shape, then fired in a continuous tunnel kiln in air or oxygen. Sintering closes the pores and the core shrinks several percent, so the tooling is deliberately oversize and the part is ground to final dimensions afterwards.

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 1-3% PVA (polyvinyl alcohol), plus 0.5-1% stearate lubricant

facts.label: Green density
facts.value: ~3.0-3.3 g/cm3 before firing

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 1100-1250 C for 1-6 h in air or O2

facts.label: Sintering shrinkage
facts.value: 12-18% linear

children.name: PVA granulation binder
children.description: Polyvinyl alcohol, made by hydrolyzing polyvinyl acetate (or by polymerising vinyl acetate) in water, gives the pressed blank enough green strength to be handled without crumbling. The organic burns out completely during the firing, which is why the finished ferrite has an open pore structure.

children.name: Vinyl acetate monomer
children.description: Made by addition of acetic acid to ethylene in the presence of a palladium catalyst at 150-200 C and 10-60 bar; the acetic acid comes from methanol carbonylation of carbon monoxide. Vinyl acetate is the monomer for PVA, polyvinyl acetate and polyvinyl chloride.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CH2=CH2 + CH3COOH -> CH3COOCH=CH2, Pd catalyst, 175 C, ~25 bar

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: ethylene from naphtha cracking, acetic acid from methanol + CO

children.name: Sintered core grinding
children.description: The sintered E is diamond or carbide-wheel ground on the mating faces and the outer leg so the stack closes properly. The 1980s alternative to this was a lapped or as-pressed core, which is why cheap cores had audible air gaps.

children.name: Enamelled copper winding
children.description: The primary, the 18 V centre-tapped secondary and the 9 V output secondary are wound in layers on a moulded bobbin, with a few hundred turns of 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper wire. Layer insulation between each pass and interleaved padding between the primary and the secondaries carry the 1000-1500 V RMS of the mains.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper, roughly 500-1200 turns per winding

facts.label: Insulation class
facts.value: class H, 180 C, by virtue of the enamel

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: layer winding; primary nearest the bobbin or outermost, secondaries separated

children.name: Enamelled magnet wire
children.description: Bare copper rod drawn down to 0.25-0.4 mm through a series of tungsten-carbide or diamond dies, then coated in two or more passes of a thermosetting enamel - typically polyester-imide (Grade 2 / THEIC) - and baked to cure it. Each coat adds roughly 5-10 um, so a double-grade wire has 25-40% more copper per given window area than bare wire.

facts.label: Wire diameter
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm bare, 0.28-0.45 mm with enamel

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyester-imide, 2 coats, ~35-45 um total build

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 160-200 C oven, 5-10 h depending on line speed

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: Grade 2 = ~2x the diameter in insulation for the same wire

children.name: Wire drawing
children.description: A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

facts.label: Start
facts.value: 8 mm rod, ~99.99% copper

facts.label: Anneal
facts.value: 500-700 C continuous bright anneal, water-cooled

facts.label: Draw passes
facts.value: 10-15 dies for 8 mm to 0.3 mm

facts.label: Final tensile strength
facts.value: ~350-450 MPa for magnet wire

children.name: Polyester-imide enamel coating
children.description: The wire runs continuously through a die-casting oven where a 25-30% solids solution of the modified polyester-imide resin in cresol/xylene is applied, then through a 350-450 C curing oven, and through the same pair again for a second coat. The thermal cure crosslinks the resin to a hard film that resists varnish, oil and coolant.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 2 (Grade 2), 3 (Grade 3)

facts.label: Build
facts.value: 35-45 um for Grade 2 at 0.3 mm

facts.label: Cure oven
facts.value: 350-450 C, 20-40 s per coat

children.name: Polyester-imide resin
children.description: The workhorse magnet-wire enamel of the 1980s. The base is a polycondensation of dimethyl terephthalate (or trimellitic anhydride) with polyols; the imide is introduced with a polyamide of trimellitic anhydride and a diamine such as ethylenediamine, which is what raises the class to H (180 C).

facts.label: Class
facts.value: H (180 C continuous)

facts.label: Key monomers
facts.value: trimellitic anhydride, terephthalic acid derivatives, diamines

children.name: Trimellitic anhydride feedstock
children.description: The 1980s industrial route to trimellitic anhydride was liquid-phase air oxidation of pseudocumene (1,2,4-trimethylbenzene), which is itself a product of the catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction of petroleum naphtha. The 1980s chemistry is what makes this enamel a petroleum-derived product rather than a coal-tar one.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: pseudocumene + air, cobalt/manganese acetate catalyst, 150-180 C

facts.label: Yield basis
facts.value: ~1.0 kg TMA per 1.0 kg pseudocumene

children.note: A coal-tar/cresol route to trimellitic anhydride existed and was used into the 1990s; the pseudocumene oxidation route became dominant in the 1980s.

children.name: Copper feedstock
children.description: Wire rod copper begins as blister copper from a copper smelter-flour mill, which begins as copper sulphide concentrate.

children.name: Copper concentrate (chalcopyrite)
children.description: Froth flotation of a porphyry copper ore, typically 20-40% Cu. The concentrate is smelted in a flash furnace to a 50-70% copper matte, converted in a converter to blister copper at 1250-1300 C, and cast.

facts.label: Concentrate grade
facts.value: 20-40 wt% Cu

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: chalcopyrite Cu5FeS2, covellite, bornite, chalcocite

children.name: Porphyry copper ore
children.description: The run-of-mine ore is a heavily disseminated sulphide system in an igneous intrusion. It is mined by open pit or block caving, crushed, and ground in SAG and ball mills to about 50-70% passing 100 microns so that the collector can float the sulphides.

facts.label: Grinding fineness
facts.value: ~100 um for flotation

children.name: Froth flotation
children.description: The ground ore is mixed with reagents - a xanthate collector, a frother such as pine oil or MIBC, and a depressant for iron sulphides - and air is blown through a bank of cells. The sulphide particles adhere to the rising bubbles and are carried off as froth, while the gangue falls to the bottom. Recovery on a porphyry concentrate in the 1980s was 80-90% with a concentrate grade of 20-40% copper.

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: xanthate or dibutyl xanthate, ~5-30 mg/L

facts.label: Frother
facts.value: pine oil, cresol or methyl isobutyl carbinol

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 80-90% into a 20-40% Cu concentrate

children.name: Moulded nylon bobbin
children.description: A spool-shaped coil former in glass-filled or unfilled nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, with cheek flanges that locate it on the core leg and a continuous slot that keeps the layer insulation in place. Bobbins were (and still are) a Miles-Platts product line, which fits the 'MP' mark found on this transformer.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, sometimes 30% glass filled

facts.label: Process
facts.value: injection moulding, 2.5-5 mm wall

children.name: Nylon 6 (polycaprolactam)
children.description: The older and cheaper of the two bobbins materials. Kaprolactam is made by the Beckmann rearrangement of cyclohexanone, which itself comes from the catalytic air oxidation of cyclohexane, which comes from benzene hydrogenation, which comes from toluene or from a naphtha cracker.

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: caprolactam (epsilon-caprolactam)

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: benzene -> cyclohexane -> cyclohexanone -> caprolactam -> polymer

children.name: Benzene from petroleum
children.description: The 1980s route to benzene was catalytic reforming of naphtha (a C6-C8 fraction of crude) over platinum on alumina at 450-520 C, which aromatises the naphthenes and paraffins; benzene is then separated by extractive distillation with sulfolane or n-heptane. A minority came from coal-tar benzene well into the 1980s.

facts.label: Benzene yield
facts.value: ~50-60% from a naphtha cut

children.name: Injection moulding the bobbin
children.description: Nylon is hygroscopic so the pellets are dried at 80 C for 4-8 h before moulding, then injection moulded at 240-280 C into a multi-cavity tool with hot runners and a mould temperature of 60-90 C. The mould cavity is polished because a flash of loose fibre on the winding slot would be a turn-coat defect.

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: 80 C, 4-8 h to <0.1% moisture

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: 60-90 C, to crystallise the nylon

children.name: Layer and interwinding insulation
children.description: Crepe paper or glass-cloth tape between winding layers, a wide kraft or composite tape wrap between the primary and the secondaries, and in the potted builds strips of polyimide (Kapton) film around the whole winding. The 1983-84 bricks visibly used masking tape on the core yoke edges and something like Kapton over the coil to keep the epoxy pour off the windings.

facts.label: Layer insulation
facts.value: crepe paper or muslin/glass cloth, ~0.2 mm

facts.label: Interwinding
facts.value: kraft-paper laminate or glass-cloth tape, 1-3 layers

facts.label: Creepage across windings
facts.value: 2-4 mm, set by the safety standard rather than by physics

children.name: Crepe paper insulation
children.description: A lightly crinkled, unbleached kraft paper that stretches to follow the winding contour without bunching. Made on a Fourdrinier machine from a dilute suspension of long-fibre softwood pulp.

children.name: Mechanical wood pulp
children.description: Softwood (spruce/fir) is debarked, chipped, steamed and refined in a disc or refiner mill; the long fibres are ideal for electrical insulation paper because they give high dielectric strength and mechanical strength in the thin sheet.

children.name: Process water and whitewater
children.description: Paper machines consume enormous volumes of water: several tonnes per tonne of pulp, treated at the mill with alum, rosin and starch, then clarified in a primary settling basin and recirculated.

children.name: Softwood pulp
children.description: The species matters as much as the process: long-fibre softwood pulp from spruce, fir or pine gives the dielectric strength and tear resistance that electrical insulation paper needs, while hardwood pulp from birch or aspen gives opacity and printability and is used in the thinner papers. Softwood is bought as chips or as market pulp.

facts.label: Fibre length
facts.value: 2-4 mm for softwood, 1-2 mm for hardwood

facts.label: Electrical grade
facts.value: low-conductivity ash and low iron content are specified

children.name: Glass-cloth insulation tape
children.description: Woven E-glass yarn cloth, ~0.1 mm thick, silane-sized for adhesion, wound in the last layer before the outer tape. Glass has no moisture absorption and much higher dielectric strength than paper, which is why the safety-approved design puts it nearest the primary.

facts.label: Yarn
facts.value: E-glass (borosilicate, ~0.5-1.5% alkali), 204-136 tex

facts.label: Dielectric strength
facts.value: >10 kV/mm in the finished laminate

children.name: E-glass fibre from molten glass
children.description: A sand/coke/limestone batch is melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C, drawn into bushings, and attenuated with air and water jets into 3-20 um filaments, then sized with silane and a PVA size. The filaments are gathered into rovings, then woven on a rapier loom into cloth.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: ~60% silica sand, 15% dolomite/limestone, 14% coke, 1% alumina/iron

facts.label: Weave
facts.value: plain or 2x2 twill, 8-19 ends/cm

children.name: Polyimide (Kapton) film
children.description: A 12-25 um amber polyimide film used as the barrier between the coil and the epoxy pour and, in later builds, as the layer insulation. Its value is that it does not soften, dissolve or outgas in a hot epoxy cure.

children.name: Pyromellitic dianhydride monomer
children.description: The diacid anhydride half of Kapton is made by air oxidation of pseudocumene to trimellitic acid and then dehydrating it - a petroleum-aromatics chain. The diamine half is 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine, both aromatics intermediates.

facts.label: Diamine
facts.value: 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: step-growth in dimethylacetamide at ~200-300 C

children.name: Interwinding earth screen
children.description: The protective-earth conductor is bonded to an aluminium or copper foil laid between the primary and the secondary windings - or sometimes to the transformer frame bolt. It does not leave the transformer: the earthing path is closed inside the potted block and never reaches the plastic case or the computer.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: aluminium or copper foil, 0.02-0.05 mm, lapped to a tab

facts.label: Termination
facts.value: crimp ring or soldered to the earth conductor of the line cord

children.note: Observed on the 902503-02: the protective-earth pin 'somehow connects to the transformer, looks like it goes in the layer between the primary and secondary winding', and does not extend to the output. The brick is all-plastic, so there is nothing to bond earth to on the outside.

children.name: Layer winding on a coil winder
children.description: A single-spindle or two-spindle coil winder turns the bobbin while traversing the wire, and the operator lays interleaved insulation between each layer with a slow-moving 'paper feeder'. Bobbin layers are counter-wound to flatten the coil, and the leads are brought out through the bobbin flange and dressed so they cannot chafe on the core.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: single- or twin-spindle coil winding machine, 1500-4000 rpm

facts.label: Traverse
facts.value: cambered (offset) layers to give a level coil

facts.label: Tension
facts.value: ~50-150 g on 0.3 mm wire

children.name: Lead termination and crimped flag terminals
children.description: The winding leads are soldered or, in the 1983-84 bricks, soldered directly to the transformer's own pins; the line cord and interwinding conductors terminate in tin-plated brass crimp flags. Under the epoxy pour the crimps are the weak link - they can anneal and let go - and the PVC of the line cord is visibly browned right at the pin.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: tin-plated brass crimp flag or ring, ~6-8 mm2 wire

facts.label: Termination to transformer
facts.value: soldered to the bobbin-terminal pins on most builds

children.note: Crimping a soldered conductor into a screw terminal is explicitly discouraged by the repair community because the soft solder creeps and the joint goes high-resistance.

children.name: Polyester varnish impregnation and oven cure
children.description: The finished assembly is vacuum impregnated with a thermosetting polyester or epoxy varnish so the winding becomes a solid block and cannot move at 50 Hz. Viscous impregnating varnishes were standard by the early 1980s; the alternative is dip-and-bake in an epoxy or a polyurethane.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: vacuum (30-50 mbar) then atmospheric impregnation

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: unsaturated polyester in styrene, or epoxy

children.name: Impregnating varnish
children.description: A low-viscosity, high-solids unsaturated polyester resin dissolved in styrene, with an organic peroxide cure catalyst. It cures by crosslinking rather than by solvent loss, so it shrinks very little and fills completely.

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 60-70 wt% in styrene

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150 C, 6-10 h; gel time minutes at 150 C

children.name: Styrene monomer
children.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene, which is made by alkylating benzene with ethylene. Again a petroleum-aromatics chain.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: benzene + ethylene -> ethylbenzene -> dehydrogenation -> styrene

children.name: Transformer pin terminal board
children.description: A row of brass pins on a small phenolic or nylon board carrying the primary, the interwinding earth, and all the secondary taps. The rectifier diodes and fuses in the 1983-84 bricks are soldered straight onto these pins, which is why the schematic 'terminals' that appear in a teardown are the transformer's own pins rather than a separate board.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 8-12 brass pins on 2.54 mm pitch

facts.label: Board material
facts.value: phenolic (paper/phenol formaldehyde) or nylon

facts.label: 902503-02 numbering
facts.value: pins 6/7/8 = centre-tapped 18 V; pins 9/11 = 9 V AC; 10 and 12 = unused spares

children.name: Phenolic laminate board
children.description: Paper or cotton-linen web impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin under heat and pressure. Cheap, dimensionally stable and self-extinguishing, which is why it was the default material for transformer terminal boards and fuseholders.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: phenol-formaldehyde, paper or cotton web

facts.label: UL flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB at typical resin content

children.name: Phenol-formaldehyde resin
children.description: Condensation polymerisation of phenol with formaldehyde, catalysed by acid or base, typically 6-9 phenol to 1 formaldehyde. Phenol itself was made in the 1980s by cumene hydroperoxide cleavage from the cumene/propylene-aromatics complex, so this too is a co-product of petroleum refining.

facts.label: Phenol route
facts.value: cumene (from benzene + propylene) -> cumene hydroperoxide -> phenol + acetone

children.name: Transformer final test
children.description: Every wound transformer is tested before it is potted or assembled: a 1500-2500 V AC dielectric withstand between primary and all secondaries, an insulation-resistance check, turns-ratio and phasing checks between the taps, and a loaded run at nominal line voltage to check regulation and temperature rise. A transformer that passes can still be potted badly, which is exactly what Commodore did.

facts.label: Dielectric withstand
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC, 1 s (unlisted components), per UL 478 / IEC 65 practice

facts.label: Insulation resistance
facts.value: >=2 MOhm at 500 V DC

facts.label: Ratio check
facts.value: secondary voltage within +/-5% at rated load

children.note: UL 478 is the US standard for power supply units; in Europe the equivalent regime was VDE 0871/EN 41003 and the household-equipment safety standard IEC 65 (BS 415 in the UK), all of which specify the same 1500 V basic dielectric withstand for a 250 V secondary circuit.

children.name: Rectifier diodes, 400GI / 1N5400
children.description: Two or four stud-less axial rectifier diodes convert the 18 V centre-tapped secondary into pulsating DC. The 902503-02 uses two General Electric 400GI silicon rectifiers in a full-wave centre-tapped configuration, which saves the two extra dice of a bridge; other builds use four 1N5400s or a moulded bridge. The diodes are soldered directly onto the transformer pins.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: GE 400GI (as marked on the 902503-02) or 1N5400, 3 A class

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: full-wave centre-tapped (2 diodes) on the 902503-02; some builds use a 4-diode bridge

facts.label: Vf at 1 A
facts.value: ~0.9-1.1 V for a 1N5400; the 400GI is noticeably slower and hotter

children.note: The 400GI is a slow-recovery rectifier with a large forward drop for its rating; hobbyists have observed it running well outside its current specification, and it is a recurring failure item. The correct part for the job is a 1N5400.

children.name: Axial rectifier diode
children.description: A single silicon junction in an axial package with a formed lead, cathode band marked with a stripe. Inside: a die a few hundred microns across with a heavy anode metallisation, a glass passivation, and epoxy or a voidless glass body filled with silicone stress-relief gel to survive the power cycling.

facts.label: Vceo / Vrrm
facts.value: 50-100 V reverse for a 400GI; 100 V for 1N5400

facts.label: If (av)
facts.value: 3 A at 75 C lead temperature for a 1N5400

facts.label: Body
facts.value: epoxy-filled axial (DO-201AD) or glass-butt

children.name: Silicon rectifier die
children.description: A 100-150 mm wafer ground to a die typically 2 x 2 x 0.3 mm, with a diffused N-type cathode and metallised anode. The same Czochralski silicon as the VIC-II and the 6510; the detailed wafer process belongs to the silicon branch of this tree.

facts.label: Junction depth
facts.value: ~20-40 um phosphorus diffusion

facts.label: Die
facts.value: ~2 x 2 mm after dicing

children.name: Silicon metal from quartz
children.description: The only starting point is high-purity quartz. Coke and quartz are carbothermically reduced in an arc furnace at 1800-2000 C to 97-99% metallurgical-grade silicon, then upgraded in a bed-type fluidised reactor to 9-11N (99.9999999%) polycrystalline silicon by trichlorosilane disproportionation or silane decomposition, which is the material pulled into a single Czochralski crystal, sawn into wafers, and polished.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO at 1800-2000 C, ~97-99% pure Si

facts.label: Wafer
facts.value: 100-150 mm Czochralski <111>

children.name: High-purity quartz (SiO2)
children.description: Quartz is dug from pegmatite or high-purity veins, crushed and acid-leached, then hydrothermally or flame fused to remove the last few ppm of aluminium, boron and iron. The semiconductor industry needs 99.99%+ SiO2 as the feed to the arc furnace.

facts.label: Purity required
facts.value: 99.99% SiO2 (metallurgical Si) -> 9-11N metal

children.name: Die attach, wire bond and axial encapsulation
children.description: The die is die-attached to the anode lead with silver-loaded glass or a soft solder, one or two aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the cathode metallisation to the cathode lead, then the whole assembly is transfer-moulded or cast in an epoxy body filled with silicone gel to relieve the thermal cycle between the glass and the leads.

facts.label: Die attach
facts.value: silver-glass die attach at 430 C, or 80Au/20Sn solder reflow at 220 C

facts.label: Wire bond
facts.value: aluminium, 50-150 um diameter, ultrasonic wedge bond, 50-250 g

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: epoxy or glass preform moulded at 150-175 C

children.name: Moulded bridge rectifier alternative
children.description: Some builds and most replacement supplies use a packaged bridge: four dice mounted on a common ceramic or moulded body with the terminals formed into the four corners. Commodore's own choice of two discrete diodes over a bridge saved two dice and one package, at the cost of a centre tap on the transformer.

facts.label: Bridge
facts.value: e.g. Varo VMO8, listed in the C64 service manual parts list as CR4 with Commodore stock number 906129-01

children.name: 5 V linear voltage regulator
children.description: The pass element that turns roughly 8-10 V of pulsating DC into 5.00 V. Three different implementations appear in C64 bricks inside two years, and the choice of which one determines how much heat has to be removed. At full load the drop across the pass device is 3-5 V at 1.5 A, so 4.5-7.5 W has to go into the heatsink - which is why these supplies run hot and why the electrolytics above them cook.

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: ~3 W at 8 V in / 1 A out; ~8 W at 10.4 V in / 1.4 A out

facts.label: Efficiency
facts.value: ~40-50% for the whole brick, dominated by the series pass

children.note: The failure mode that destroyed C64s is the pass device shorting the input to the output, putting ~8-10 V on a rail designed for 5 V. Unloaded 5.3 V is normal; 5.4 V is the number to worry about; below 4.6 V the machine will not boot.

children.name: 7805-class three-pin regulator
children.description: The simplest form: a monolithic regulator containing the reference, error amplifier, current limit and the pass transistor, in a TO-220 or TO-3P-like plastic body with a tab bolted to the heatsink. In the 251053-02 brick it is a three-legged part with rectangular legs, screwed straight into the folded aluminium plate under a blob of epoxy.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V, 1.5 A continuous for a 7805 in a TO-220 with a small copper tab

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: internally ~2.2 A thermal-limited foldback

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: single bolt through the tab into the heatsink plate

children.name: Sanken SI-3052P integrated regulator
children.description: The regulator in the later 902503-02, which many hobbyists misidentify as a transistor because it is moulded in a TO-3P-looking package. It is a 5 V / 2 A linear regulator with an internal error amplifier and a foldback current limit that kicks in at about 2.4 A. The datasheet explicitly warns that the output must not be raised by inserting a resistor in the ground pin - and Commodore inserted a 300 Ohm resistor in the ground pin anyway, to make up for the drop in the output cable.

facts.label: Maker
facts.value: Sanken Electric (the 'SK' in the part number is Sanken's logo)

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V fixed, 2 A

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: ~2.4 A foldback

facts.label: Ground-lift resistor
facts.value: 300 Ohm nominal (some builds 30 Ohm) from the regulator ground pin to the output return

children.note: The ground-lift trick raises the output a few tens of millivolts to compensate for the resistive drop of a metre of thin output wire, but it also corrupts the regulator's ground reference and interferes with its current-limit behaviour - the datasheet says so in Note 3. Modifying this circuit is the standard modern replacement and is well documented.

children.name: Output stability capacitor
children.description: A small electrolytic or tantalum directly across the regulator's input and output pins. The datasheet requires it for loop stability; a 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum appears on some 902503-02 builds and the 3-83 version has the holes for it but does not populate it, which suggests it was a late cost change.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum (populated on some builds, holes only on others)

children.name: Discrete 2N3055 / 2N3792 series-pass regulator
children.description: The earliest 'repairable' silver-label brick used a discrete design: an NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can bolted to a heatsink as the series pass, a smaller driver transistor, a zener or low-current regulator as the reference, wirewound resistors in the emitter and base for current limiting, and a thermal shutdown in contact with the heatsink. It is the arrangement the 902503-02's monolithic regulator replaced.

facts.label: Pass transistor
facts.value: 2N3055 (15 A / 60 V, TO-3) or 2N3792 (1.5 A class NPN, TO-3)

facts.label: Vbe multiplier error amp
facts.value: two-transistor error amplifier sensing the output through a divider

facts.label: Emitter ballast
facts.value: wirewound resistor to force a minimum standing current and to limit current sharing

children.note: I could not reach a verified transcription of the 120407 discrete-regulator schematic (lemon64's forum is behind a bot challenge). The topology and part families described here are the standard 1982 discrete 5 V linear supply of this size; treat the exact part numbers as unconfirmed for this specific assembly.

children.name: 2N3055 / 2N3792 power NPN
children.description: A triple-diffused planar NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can: a bolted metal header with an isolation disc, the die brazed or soldered to the header, one or two emitter bonds, and a hermetic can with a glass-sealed pin feedthrough. The 2N3055 is grossly oversized for a 1.5 A load (15 A, 60 V, 115 W dissipation capability), which is exactly why it was chosen: it could not fail thermally even when the circuit was badly designed.

facts.label: 2N3055
facts.value: NPN, 15 A Ic, 60 V Vceo, Pc 115 W with a good heat sink

facts.label: 2N3792
facts.value: NPN power transistor, roughly 1.5 A / 60 V class, TO-3

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: triple-diffused planar (collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter diffusions)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-3 can, 40-60 g of nickel-plated copper, mica or thin mica-fibre washer under the can

children.note: Modern practice for a 1.5 A rail is an 8-20 A TO-220 or a DPAK/LDO with an active current limit; the 2N3055 in a TO-3 is expensive and a thermal mismatch, but it was the safest thing an engineer could buy off the shelf in 1982.

children.name: Triple-diffused planar process
children.description: Three sequential dopings - collector-base, base-emitter, and a deep collector-emitter - through a photolithographically masked oxide. The heavy collector-emitter diffusion carries the load current while the shallow, tightly controlled base-emitter diffusion sets the gain and the breakdown voltage. This is the process that made 15 A transistors possible at all.

facts.label: Diffusions
facts.value: collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter (P, B, B, P)

facts.label: Base-emitter depth
facts.value: ~1-2 um; collector-emitter ~20-40 um

facts.label: Die
facts.value: typically 100 x 100 mm wafer, diced into 6 x 6 mm TO-3 dice

children.name: Die attach and hermetic TO-3 sealing
children.description: The die is brazed to the header in a hydrogen atmosphere at 700-800 C with an active-metal braze, or soldered with a 50Pb-50Sn or AuSn preform at 220-300 C; the header is then nickel-plated. The can is crimped or cold-welded onto the header with an annular glass or ceramic feedthrough insulator; mica or a thin mica-fibre washer goes between the can and the heatsink to isolate the collector while conducting heat.

facts.label: Brazing
facts.value: Ni-B or Au-Ag, 700-800 C, dry H2

facts.label: Feedthrough
facts.value: glass ring or BeO disc, 20-30 um seal gap

facts.label: Can
facts.value: nickel-plated low-carbon steel, cold-welded (soft solder) or crimped (hard solder)

children.name: Emitter wire bonds
children.description: Two to four 100-200 um aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the emitter metallisation to the emitter lead to carry the full emitter current; the collector current flows through the die's back contact straight into the header. Ultrasonic wedge bonding at 50-250 g per wire was the universal method - ball bonding was for fine-pitch.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 100-200 um aluminium, 99.99% Al + small Mg

facts.label: Force
facts.value: 50-250 g ultrasonic

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: 2-4 in parallel on the emitter for a 15 A device

children.name: Driver / error-amplifier transistor
children.description: A small-signal NPN whose job is to supply the ~0.7 V of base drive plus the feedback signal the pass transistor needs. In a 1982 discrete supply this is typically a TO-92 part with hFE around 100-400, or one half of a matched pair. Its collector dissipation is small but its junction temperature is close to the pass transistor's, so it shares the same heatsink metal.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: TO-92 small-signal NPN, e.g. 2N3904 / BC547 class

facts.label: Base drive
facts.value: ~0.6-0.8 V above the pass emitter, set by the Vbe multiplier

children.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2N3904 and 2N4401 in TO-92 packages for its audio and cassette motor drives (Q1-Q8 in the 326298 parts list), so the same parts bins would have supplied the brick.

children.name: Voltage reference
children.description: In a 1982 discrete supply the reference is either a 5.1-6.2 V zener diode biased from a constant-current source, or a low-current three-terminal regulator such as a TL431 or a small 7805 in a TO-92 used purely as a reference. The zener route needs a stable bias current; the temperature coefficient of an ordinary zener is poor, which shows up as output drift with case temperature.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~0.1%/C for an uncompensated zener vs ~0.005%/C for a bandgap reference

children.note: Modern practice is a bandgap reference inside the regulator IC, giving ±0.5% over temperature; the zener plus Vbe-multiplier arrangement of 1982 gave ±3-5% and drifted with case temperature.

children.name: Emitter ballast resistors
children.description: One to three wirewound resistors in series with the pass transistor's emitter. Their purpose is to develop a signal proportional to output current for current limiting and to force a standing current through the pass transistor so its hFE and therefore the loop gain do not collapse at light load. Wirewound rather than film because the dissipation is fractional watts but the temperature rise has to stay small.

facts.label: Values
facts.value: 0.1-1 Ohm, 1-3 W wirewound, manganin or constantan

facts.label: Temperature coefficient
facts.value: chosen near zero for manganin, positive for constantan

children.note: Ballast resistors were largely abandoned in integrated regulators because the current-limit loop senses the emitter directly through a pin.

children.name: Manganin wire
children.description: A copper-manganese-nickel alloy (typically 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni) whose resistivity barely changes with temperature. A spiral-wound wirewound resistor is made by winding manganin or constantan wire onto a ceramic or plastic former and baking it under high tension so the winding stress-relaxes and stays against the form.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: ~86 Cu / 12 Mn / 2 Ni (manganin) or ~60 Cu / 40 Ni (constantan)

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: <10 ppm/K for manganin

children.name: Thermal shutdown
children.description: A temperature-sensitive element in contact with the heatsink - a thermistor or a bimetallic thermal switch - that shorts or removes the driver bias when the sink passes roughly 90-110 C, so the supply folds back rather than destroying itself. Commodore's bricks more often relied on a thermal fuse in the primary and on the epoxy pot for heat retention, which is the root of their reputation.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~95-110 C typical for a thermal switch

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: bimetal opens a contact, or an SCR crowbar latches a short

children.note: The 251053-02 teardowns document a thermal fuse in series with the primary winding but I did not find a documented thermal shutdown switch inside the regulator board.

children.name: NTC thermistor
children.description: A bead or disc of semiconducting metal oxide whose resistance falls steeply with temperature (10 kOhm at 25 C, ~1 kOhm at 100 C for the standard 10K curve). Glued or bolted to the heatsink and shunting the driver bias, it gives a soft, non-resetting protection that must cool before it re-conducts.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 10 kOhm at 25 C, B = 3435 K curve

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ferric oxide or manganese oxide semiconducting ceramic

children.name: Bolting the regulator to the heatsink
children.description: The regulator tab or TO-3 can is bolted to the folded aluminium plate with a thin layer of thermal compound - in 1982 typically a zinc-oxide paste in a silicone or hydrocarbon base, or sometimes simply a piece of thin copper foil. The thermal interface matters more than the compound brand: dry metal-to-metal contact is roughly ten times worse than a properly filled joint.

facts.label: Torque
facts.value: ~0.3-0.5 Nm on an M3 screw for a TO-3; overtightening cracks the can

facts.label: Interface
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 mm thermal grease, or a thin copper shim

facts.label: Isolator
facts.value: mica or silicone-rubber washer under a TO-3 collector tab

children.note: The 251053-02 teardown shows the heatsink as a 'featureless aluminium plate bent into a U-shape' with a drilled and tapped hole for the regulator screw; a drill bit slipped into the soft aluminium and had to be drilled out from several angles, which is a good illustration of how thin and soft the sink actually is.

children.name: Folded aluminium heatsink
children.description: A thin aluminium plate folded into a U so that one leg clamps under the case and the other presents an area against the regulator. There are no fins: the design relies on the natural convection of a brick sitting under a desk. It is the reason the case runs at 60-70 C and the epoxy never fully cools.

facts.label: Geometry
facts.value: flat sheet folded into a U, ~1-2 mm thick, no fins

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: 3-8 W at a 35-45 C rise above ambient

facts.label: Material
facts.value: commercial-purity aluminium, mill finish or painted

children.note: Modern practice would use an extruded finned profile in 6063 aluminium; a folded sheet U gives only 0.02-0.04 m2 of surface, an order of magnitude less than the fins a switching supply would use for the same power.

children.name: Sheet folding and tapping
children.description: Strip or sheet is blanked, then folded on a press brake to a U; the mounting hole is punched or drilled and tapped with a thread-forming tap. Aluminium's low modulus means the fold must be given a generous inside radius or the sheet tears, and the tapped hole must be at least 1.5 diameters from the bend.

facts.label: Fold radius
facts.value: >=1.5 t inside radius

facts.label: Thread
facts.value: M3 or M4 roll-tapped (form tap) to avoid chipping the threads

children.name: Aluminium sheet and its ore
children.description: Commercial-purity aluminium sheet is made from an electrolytic ingot of 99.0-99.7% aluminium, which is refined from alumina dissolved in cryolite.

children.name: Smelter-grade alumina
children.description: Aluminium oxide obtained by the Bayer process from bauxite. The ore is crushed, digested in hot caustic soda under pressure, the insoluble red mud is separated by settling, and alumina is precipitated from the clarified sodium aluminate by cooling and seeding, then calcined at 1000-1100 C.

facts.label: Digestion
facts.value: 150-250 C, caustic soda, autoclave

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: ~99.5% Al2O3 for smelting feed

children.name: Bauxite
children.description: The aluminium ore, 30-60% Al2O3 with up to 50% Fe2O3 and SiO2, dug from tropical laterite and bauxite terraces. This is the leaf of the aluminium chain.

facts.label: Major impurities
facts.value: Fe2O3 (red colour), SiO2, TiO2

children.note: Guinea (Boke), Australia (Weipa, Gove) and Jamaica were the dominant 1982 sources. This is the leaf of the aluminium branch.

children.name: Bauxite mining and washing
children.description: Bauxite is dug from shallow open pits in tropical laterite caps, typically only 5-20 m of overburden, then crushed and washed. The Bayer process is defeated by high silica, so the ore is beneficiated: scrubbed and screened to remove the clay, and often upgraded by gravity separation. The waste is red mud - a thick alkaline sludge held in ponds.

facts.label: Overburden
facts.value: 5-20 m of soil over the bauxite horizon

facts.label: Rejection
facts.value: ore above roughly 4-6% reactive silica is rejected for the Bayer process

facts.label: Red mud
facts.value: ~1-2 t of alkaline residue per tonne of alumina produced

children.name: Laterite and bauxite geology
children.description: Bauxite is not a mineral but a rock: a residual soil that forms when tropical weathering leaches silica and alkalis out of aluminous parent rock, leaving the insoluble alumina and iron behind as hard concretions. That is why bauxite only forms within about 30 degrees of the equator and why the deposits sit as blankets on old erosion surfaces rather than as veins.

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: intense chemical weathering of aluminous parent rock in the tropics

facts.label: Typical mineralogy
facts.value: gibbsite Al(OH)3 with minor boehmite and diaspore

facts.label: Gibbsite dehydration
facts.value: above ~300 C gibbsite converts to boehmite, which is harder to digest

children.name: Caustic soda for digestion
children.description: The Bayer process reagent, made by the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine. It is recovered from the red-mud wash liquor and recycled, so a 1980s alumina plant consumed a few hundred kg of net Na2O per tonne of alumina.

facts.label: Net consumption
facts.value: ~100-250 kg Na2CO3 equivalent per tonne alumina

children.name: Hall-Heroult electrolysis
children.description: Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite at 950-970 C and electrolytically reduced; molten aluminium collects on the carbon-lined cathode and is tapped every one or two days. A modern pot consumes 13,000-15,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium, essentially all of it as thermal/electrical energy from a dedicated power station.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ~13,000-15,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Carbon anodes
facts.value: consumed, ~0.4-0.5 t per tonne of aluminium, making pot alumina the main waste

children.name: Anodising or painting the heatsink
children.description: A black anodised or painted surface raises the emissivity enough to improve radiation heat transfer a little, but on a folded sheet with no fins the benefit is marginal. Anodising is a sulphuric or chromic acid bath at 20 C with a few volts across the part, growing a thin aluminium oxide film.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sulphuric acid, 20 C, 1-2 V/0.5-1 A/dm2

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 5-25 um, sealed in boiling water

children.name: 4700 uF 16 V aluminium electrolytic
children.description: The single reservoir capacitor on the rectifier output. It is the part that has killed the most C64s: as the electrolyte dries out the ripple current is no longer smoothed, the series regulator loses headroom and starts pumping 100/120 Hz ripple onto the 5 V rail, and eventually the cap leaks current into the regulator's ground reference and pushes the output up past 5.5 V. Replacements are still sold as the C64 'fix' four decades later.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 4700 uF / 16 V radial (2200 uF in some builds; 2200 uF / 16 V on the C64 mainboard itself)

facts.label: Lifetime
facts.value: rated 2000 h at 85 C; real service life 10-20 years at 40 C ambient

children.note: Two capacitors in parallel have lower ESR than either alone, which is why both the replacement-PSU literature and the datasheets push for two. Failure is not dramatic: capacitance drifts down, ESR climbs, ripple appears, and eventually the leakage current rises far enough to upset the regulator.

children.name: Aluminium anode foil
children.description: The anode is a 12-20 um aluminium foil that has been chemically etched in a hot chlorate or permanganate bath to roughen the surface into a high-area sponge. Because capacitance is proportional to real surface area, the etch multiplies the effective area by 30-100x and is the entire reason a 4700 uF part fits in a 25 mm can.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: 12-20 um for the anode; 6-9 um for the cathode

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: NaClO3/HCl or KMnO4 at 70-80 C for 10-60 min

facts.label: Surface gain
facts.value: 30-100x the geometrical area; pore size 0.5-2 um

children.note: For low-voltage parts the etched foil was often replaced in the late 1980s by a laser-drilled or plasma-etched solid aluminium can, which is the modern practice.

children.name: Rolling aluminium foil to 12-20 um
children.description: Cast rolling ingot is hot rolled to a few mm in a reversing mill, then cold rolled in a Sendzimir or 20-high mill to 0.05 mm and finally foil rolled to 12-20 um. Foil rolling is done dry or with a light kerosene/paraffin lubricant, and the last pass determines the tensile strength and the pinholes - a pinhole becomes a short, which is why foil is rolled in the tightest gauges last.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: ingot -> hot roll 6 mm -> cold roll -> 12-20 um

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: kerosene or paraffin for the final pass

facts.label: Tensile strength at 12 um
facts.value: ~80-140 MPa, work-hardened

children.name: Chemical etching of the anode foil
children.description: The foil is threaded continuously through an etch tank at 70-80 C. Sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid, or potassium permanganate, dissolves aluminium faster where the surface is already rough, so the etch runs away into a deep microscopic pore structure rather than eating away uniformly. The etched foil is rinsed, dried and cut to length.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: NaClO3 + HCl, or KMnO4 in an alkaline bath

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 10-60 min depending on the required pore depth

children.name: Potassium permanganate etchant
children.description: An alkaline potassium permanganate bath oxidises the aluminium surface; the loose MnO2 sludge is removed by brushing or a nitric acid dip. The alternative chlorate chemistry was being phased out for safety and environmental reasons through the 1980s because chlorate/dioxide is toxic.

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: ~2-6% KMnO4 plus NaOH

children.note: The chlorate etch was being displaced by the permanganate and by mechanical/electrochemical etching through the mid-1980s.

children.name: Electrolytic formation of the anode oxide
children.description: The wound wet cell is energised from a DC source at a voltage ramped up to the rated working voltage. At the anode the aluminium oxidises to a dense amorphous alumina film only a few nanometres thick - the dielectric. Raising the voltage thickens the film; raising the temperature thickens it faster but also lets it dissolve, which is why forming is done hot and forming voltage is always lower than the operating voltage.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~1.1-1.3x the rated voltage, ramped over 1-4 h

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: 2-5 nm of amorphous Al2O3 at 16 V rating

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~8-10 for amorphous alumina

children.name: Electrolytic electrolyte
children.description: An aqueous solution of an ammonium or amine salt - ammonium pentaborate was the classic low-voltage recipe - that forms the counter-electrode ion layer against the oxide. In an aluminium electrolytic the cathode reaction deposits a hydrated aluminium oxide or tin layer from the metal ion, and the leakage current is exactly that reaction rate.

facts.label: Typical system
facts.value: ammonium pentaborate / ammonium chloride, or an amine salt

facts.label: Leakage current
facts.value: I = kC V, roughly 2x the CV product rated current at 25 C

children.note: Modern practice for long-life parts is a higher-boiling organic solvent (propylene glycol, GBL esters) with a benzotriazole inhibitor instead of ammonium salts - ammonium systems dry out faster and leak more once the solvent is gone.

children.name: Cell separator
children.description: A porous dielectric sheet between the anode and the cathode foil, keeping them apart without shorting. Low-voltage parts in 1980-82 used cellulose (paper) separators, which is the direct cause of the decades-later failure: paper is hygroscopic and absorbs electrolyte, and the carbonisation of that paper when leakage current rises shorts the cell.

facts.label: 1980-82 default
facts.value: cellulose kraft separator

facts.label: Later default
facts.value: polypropylene or polyethylene, and aluminium oxide-filled separators

children.name: Polypropylene separator
children.description: The 1980s onwards replacement for paper. Made by extruding isotactic polypropylene from propylene obtained in a steam cracker, then stretching and/or solvent extraction to make a microporous film. It does not absorb electrolyte and does not carbonise into a short when it overheats.

children.name: Propylene from the steam cracker
children.description: Propane and butane from natural-gas liquids or from crude fractionation are steam cracked at 800-900 C with a residence time of under a second to give a propylene-rich C3 stream, which is then purified by selective hydrogenation or distillation. Polypropylene and acrylonitrile both start here.

facts.label: Cracker
facts.value: 800-900 C, 0.5-2 s residence, coils of 304H alloy

facts.label: Propylene yield
facts.value: ~15-25% on a propylene-propane feed

children.name: Cellulose paper separator
children.description: A thin kraft paper sheet, ~10-20 um, made on a Fourdrinier or a twin-wire machine. Absorbs electrolyte and swells; on ageing it chars and shorts. This is why a decades-old electrolytic usually fails suddenly and violently rather than just drifting.

children.name: Cellulose from wood hydrolysis
children.description: The cellulose is made by the soda or kraft process: wood chips are cooked at 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide, the lignin is washed out with the caustic liquor and burned for heat, and the remaining cellulose is bleached with chlorine or hypochlorite. A paper-grade mill in 1982 recovered well over a tonne of black liquor as fuel per tonne of pulp.

facts.label: Cooking
facts.value: 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide, 2-6 h

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: ~1.2-1.5 t black liquor per tonne of pulp, burned for process heat

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine or hypochlorite, then acid wash

children.name: Winding and impregnating the cell
children.description: The anode foil (etched) and the cathode (bare aluminium foil, or the can itself in later types) are separated by the separator and wound on a mandrel into a compact roll, the leads are brought out, and the roll is impregnated under vacuum with the electrolyte so the pores fill completely. Air left in the roll is the single biggest cause of high ESR.

facts.label: Vacuum impregnation
facts.value: ~1-10 mbar before electrolyte is admitted

facts.label: Squeeze
facts.value: rolled to expel electrolyte and set the dimensions

facts.label: Can seal
facts.value: rubber bung pressed against the leads, then a silicone or bitumen fill

children.note: Modern high-CV parts use a laser-drilled solid can as the cathode, eliminating the cathode foil and reducing ESR and inductance further.

children.name: Tantalum and small electrolytic capacitors
children.description: Secondary filtering: a 0.22 uF 35 V tantalum and a 47 uF 10 V electrolytic on the 5 V output for stability and for the load transients the VIC-II produces when it banks memory. The tantalum is polar and fails short, so it is the more dramatic failure of the pair.

facts.label: Tantalum
facts.value: 0.22 uF / 35 V, epoxy-dipped bead or drop

facts.label: Electrolytic
facts.value: 47 uF / 10 V radial

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: 100 Ohm and 22 Ohm carbon-film, embedded in the epoxy pour

children.name: Sintered tantalum bead capacitor
children.description: A porous sintered tantalum pellet, pressed from tantalum powder and sintered at 1200-2000 C under vacuum, dipped in manganese dioxide as the solid electrolyte, then coated with a conductive polymer or resin and epoxy for protection. Extremely high capacitance per unit volume and no liquid electrolyte to dry out, but it fails short and can burn.

facts.label: Anode
facts.value: sintered tantalum powder, ~99.9% Ta, grain size 1-3 um

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: manganese dioxide, grown electrochemically at 90-200 V

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-2000 C under vacuum

facts.label: CV product
facts.value: ~10,000 uF.V per cc - roughly 10x an aluminium electrolytic

children.name: Tantalum and its ore
children.description: Tantalum columbite ore (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 is mined from pegmatites in Australia, Brazil and Zaire, converted to potassium tantalofluoride K2TaF7 by caustic fusion and acid digestion, then reduced to tantalum powder with potassium as the reductant. The metal is then capacitor-grade: electron-beam or vacuum refined, and only the small crystal grains are used.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: Ta2O5 equivalent, typically 0.02-0.05% Ta2O5 in columbite

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + K -> Ta powder, 700-900 C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: electron-beam melting / electron-beam floating zone to 99.9-99.99%

children.name: Potassium reduction of K2TaF7
children.description: Calcium or potassium reduction of the double fluoride at 700-900 C under vacuum, in batches of a few hundred kilos. This is a batch chemical reduction, not a smelting process, which is why capacitor-grade tantalum was expensive and rare relative to aluminium.

children.name: Columbite-tantalite in pegmatite
children.description: The ore is a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, chemically almost identical niobium and tantalum oxides, and it concentrates in the last stages of pegmatite crystallisation. Because tantalum and niobium are so hard to separate, the industry uses fractional re-crystallisation of the fluoride: K2TaF7 and K2NbF7 have different solubilities, so repeated precipitation progressively enriches the tantalum.

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: columbite-tantalite (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6

facts.label: Host
facts.value: granitic pegmatite, worked from a few thousand tonnes of ore per tonne of Ta2O5

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: fractional re-crystallisation of K2TaF7 / K2NbF7

children.name: Small regulator PCB, 'PNE-5'
children.description: A single-sided glass-epoxy board about 40 x 30 mm carrying the regulator, the two electrolytics, the tantalum and two resistors, with the identification 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the earlier build and no marking at all on the later one. It is held in place only by the epoxy that floods the whole case, which is why de-potting usually breaks it.

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the 3-83 build; unmarked on the 13-83

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: FR-4 glass-epoxy, ~1.6 mm, single sided

children.name: FR-4 glass-epoxy laminate
children.description: Woven E-glass impregnated with brominated epoxy resin and heat-cured into a sheet. By the early 1980s FR-4 had displaced the older phenolic paper laminate (FR-2) for anything that needed dimensional stability or a higher Tg.

facts.label: Tg
facts.value: ~135-150 C for the standard mid-Tg FR-4 of the early 1980s

facts.label: Epoxy
facts.value: tetrachlorobisphenol A or brominated BPA, ~18-20% resin by weight

facts.label: UL flammability
facts.value: UL 94 V-0 at the usual resin loading

children.name: Copper-clad laminate pressing
children.description: Glass fabric is woven to a controlled thickness, impregnated with brominated epoxy in a treater, and partially cured into a B-stage prepreg. The prepreg sheets and copper foil are then stacked - typically two or four copper layers for a two-sided or four-sided board - and pressed between platens at 160-200 C and 1-3 MPa, which completes the cure and bonds the foil to the laminate. The board is then drilled, the holes plated through with copper, and the pattern etched.

facts.label: Copper foil
facts.value: 35 um (1 oz) standard, 18 um (half oz) for fine pitch

facts.label: Drill
facts.value: 0.3-0.8 mm carbide or diamond-coated bit

children.name: Epoxy potting pour
children.description: From mid-1983 Commodore filled the case with a two-part epoxy so the whole assembly became one solid block: transformer, board, fuses, leads, the lot, in a minty-green or cool-grey mass. It made the unit tamper-proof and un-serviceable, and it turned out to be the primary cause of failure because the heat of the linear regulator could no longer escape.

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: minty green (3-83) or cool grey (13-83), both indicating different epoxy batches

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: the case is filled to within a few mm of the lid, leaving only the connector, cord and switch exposed

facts.label: Repairability
facts.value: effectively zero - extraction breaks the PCB and the transformer terminals

children.note: The epoxy is also an insulator thermally as well as electrically: it fills the natural convection paths around the heatsink and the transformer, so internal temperatures run 20-40 C above what the same parts see in an open case.

children.name: Two-part epoxy chemistry
children.description: A diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A liquid resin, crosslinked with a polyamine or anhydride hardener. In an unfilled pour the potted block is a poor thermal conductor (0.2-0.4 W/m.K), so it acts as a thermal blanket around its own contents; filled versions with silica or alumina flour conduct 1-3 W/m.K and would not have had this problem.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: DGEBA (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether), epoxide value 0.52-0.57 mol/100 g

facts.label: Hardener
facts.value: triethylene tetramine (DETA) or an anhydride

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 24 h at 25 C or 2-4 h at 80 C

facts.label: Thermal conductivity
facts.value: 0.2-0.4 W/m.K unfilled; 1-3 W/m.K silica-filled

children.name: Epichlorohydrin feedstock
children.description: The other half of the bisphenol-A epoxy molecule. In the 1980s it was made by chlorination of propylene to propylene dichloride, then dehydrochlorination to allyl chloride, then addition of hypochlorous acid (from chlorine and water) to give epichlorohydrin. Both propylene and chlorine are basic chemicals.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: propylene -> propylene dichloride -> allyl chloride -> epichlorohydrin

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: 1,2-dichloropropanol, which had to be destroyed - the reason epichlorohydrin plants carried incinerators

children.name: Bisphenol A from phenol and acetone
children.description: Two moles of phenol condensed with one mole of acetone in the presence of an acid catalyst give bisphenol A. Both phenol (from cumene oxidation) and acetone (from the cumene process, or from propylene via isopropanol) are petroleum-aromatics or -ketone co-products, so the epoxy is a petroleum-derived plastic.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2 C6H5OH + (CH3)2CO -> C15H16O2 + H2O, acid catalyst

facts.label: Phenol source
facts.value: cumene hydroperoxide cleavage

children.name: Black ABS enclosure
children.description: A two-half injection-moulded case in black ABS, ~150 x 100 x 60 mm, with a tongue-and-groove seam, ribbing on the sides for stiffness, four case screws and one larger screw holding the cable clamp. On the potted builds the seam is a line of epoxy. Some units have the rating text moulded into the plastic; others have it printed on the underside and on a metallised label.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene), natural or black

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB is the normal requirement for a PSU enclosure; V-2 or V-0 is required if it is a subassembly of a listed appliance

facts.label: Markings
facts.value: moulded into the casing on the 3-83 build; printed on the underside with a metalised date sticker on the 13-83

children.note: ABS is used because it is tough, chemically inert to the epoxy and the PVC of the cord, and injection moulds to a good surface for the moulded-in lettering. It burns readily - which is why the flammability rating and the 94-HB test are part of the approval, not decoration.

children.name: UL 94 flammability test
children.description: A 125 x 13 x 13 mm bar of the plastic is held 10 mm above a burner. For the HB rating it must not burn faster than 1 mm/s over the first 100 mm. For V-2 the flame must extinguish within 30 s and the glowing material within 60 s; V-0 requires extinction within 10/30 s. Natural ABS is normally HB; flame-retardant ABS grades exist but were not used here.

facts.label: Bar
facts.value: 125 x 13 x 13 mm, conditioned 48 h at 23 C / 50% RH

facts.label: HB rate
facts.value: <= 1 mm/s over the first 100 mm

facts.label: V-0
facts.value: flame out within 10 s, no glowing after 30 s, no drips

children.name: Case screws
children.description: Cross-recessed pan-head self-tapping screws into moulded bosses in the plastic, and in a mains appliance they must be short enough that they cannot reach the primary wiring - a specific check in the safety audit.

facts.label: Fastener
facts.value: 3.5 x 10 mm pan-head cross recess, zinc-plated steel

facts.label: Safety rule
facts.value: no screw long enough to contact a live part

children.name: 6-pin DIN output connector
children.description: A moulded round DIN socket on the case face carrying the two 5 V conductors, the two 9 V AC conductors and, in the six-pin version, the second 9 V AC leg. Later builds reduced it to four pins. The C64's mainboard has the mating plug, and the two ends of the 5 V pair are deliberately larger-diameter so the plug cannot be inserted backwards.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 6 on the 120407-era and 251053-02 builds; 4 on some later revisions

facts.label: Assignment (902503-02)
facts.value: pin 2 = 0 V return, pin 5 = +5 V, pins 6 and 7 = the two 9 V AC legs

facts.label: Housing
facts.value: nylon or phenolic shell over brass pins

children.note: The 902503-02 schematic labels the output as 5 V DC 7.5A; 7.5 W (1.5 A) is the correct figure and the 'A' is a long-standing typo on Commodore's own drawing.

children.name: Connector nylon shell and brass pins
children.description: The shell is moulded from a glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF) with a chamfered keyway that defines the pin polarisation; the pins are brass, often nickel-plated for wear, and are a press-fit or riveted into the shell. The 5 V pins are larger so that the plug is keyed by power, not by numbering.

facts.label: Shell material
facts.value: PA66-GF30 or phenolic, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Pins
