facts.value: brass, 0.8-1.0 mm, nickel-plated

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: circular DIN, 180 degrees between pins

children.name: Power indicator LED
children.description: Not present on every brick. Where fitted it is a 3 mm red LED in a small nylon bezel, fed from the 5 V rail through a 330 Ohm to 1 kOhm resistor so that the constant ~7 mA is well inside the LED's safe operating current, and the resistor - not the LED - is what limits the current when the rail is at 5.4 V.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 3 mm diffused red LED, ~1.6-2.0 V forward drop

facts.label: Series resistor
facts.value: 330 Ohm - 1 kOhm carbon film

children.note: Confirmed only on some replacement bricks I read about; I did not verify a fitted LED inside an original Commodore brick, and the 251053-02 teardown photo descriptions do not mention one. The 3-83/13-83 case markings list only 'power supply', no indicator, which suggests the indicator is on later units only.

children.name: Rating label and moulded markings
children.description: The safety-critical data: input volts and frequency, VA input, 5 V DC watts, 9 V AC VA, the approval marks and the warning text. On the 3-83 build the text is moulded into the case; on the 13-83 it is printed on the underside, duplicated on a top label and given a date on a metallised sticker. Every approval scheme requires this data to be legible without opening the unit.

facts.label: 3-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 40 VA in; 5 V DC 7.5 W and 9 V AC 6.7 VA out; UL 13J5; 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: 13-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 46 W in; 5 V DC 8.5 W and 9 V AC 9 VA out; CSA and NLS marks; 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN' in English and French

children.name: Metallised polyester label
children.description: A 25 um metallised polyester film printed with one or two hit spot colours and applied with an acrylic adhesive. Metallised polyester is used because it is tear-resistant, solvent-resistant and survives the polyester solvents in the potting epoxy, unlike paper.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 25 um metallised BOPP or polyester

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: acrylic, applied by pressure-sensitive transfer

children.name: Metallised BOPP film
children.description: Biaxially oriented polypropylene film, stretched in both directions so the molecules line up to give high tensile strength and tear resistance in any direction, then vacuum-metallised with aluminium. The printing inks are solvent-based dyes and pigment pastes that are dried and overlaminated.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 20-40 um before metallisation

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: ~0.1 um of vapour-deposited aluminium

children.name: Biaxial orientation
children.description: A cast polypropylene or cast polyethylene film is stretched in the machine direction, cooled, then stretched again in the transverse direction and heat-set. The two stretching steps line the polymer chains up in both directions, so the film has high tensile strength and tear resistance whatever the pull direction - which is exactly why a torn BOPP label ends in a straight line rather than a ragged one.

facts.label: Stretch ratios
facts.value: ~3-5x machine direction, ~4-10x transverse for a label film

facts.label: Set temperature
facts.value: 110-140 C to freeze the orientation

children.name: Brick assembly and final test
children.description: The order of operations is visible in the potted builds: the transformer is soldered to by the diodes and fuses at its own pins, the small board is populated, the LED and connector are fitted, the assembly is dropped into the case, epoxy is poured, the halves are screwed together, and the finished unit is then hi-pot tested, earth-continuity tested and burned in on load. Testing after potting is what lets a potted brick be safe and unrepairable at the same time.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: transformer wiring first, then board, then connector, then pot, then close and test

facts.label: Documents required
facts.value: the safety file: schematic, PCB artwork, BOM, transformer winding instruction, insulation system drawing, critical-components list and test instructions

children.name: Hi-pot dielectric withstand test
children.description: 1-1.5 kV AC is applied between the primary and the joined secondaries for about one second, with the leakage current monitored and the test set tripping on either a flashover or an excess leakage current. It finds a pinhole in the enamel, a missing layer of insulation paper, or a solder splash bridging the bobbin.

facts.label: Trip current
facts.value: typically 5 mA for a basic-insulation product

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 50/60 Hz, or 0.1-0.5 Hz on modern electronic test sets

children.name: Protective-earth continuity test
children.description: A low current (typically 25-50 A for a Class I product, but only a few amps here) is passed from the earth pin of the line cord to the earth tab on the transformer, and the resistance must be below ~0.1 ohm. In this all-plastic brick the earth stops at the transformer, so the test is a continuity check on one bond, not on a case.

facts.label: Limit
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm between the cord earth pin and the bonded point

facts.label: Note
facts.value: there is no accessible metal enclosure to bond to

children.name: Load burn-in and temperature rise
children.description: Every unit is run at rated load - a resistive or electronic load drawing 1.5 A from the 5 V rail plus a load on the 9 V AC - for 2-8 hours while case temperature and output voltage are logged. This is the test that finds the dry solder joints and thermal-runaway designs that a 30 second hi-pot never will. Hobbyists have independently rediscovered it: stress the brick for hours, with thermal cycling, before trusting it on a C64.

facts.label: Load
facts.value: 1.5 A on 5 V plus up to 1 A on the 9 V AC winding

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 2-8 h; 8 h with thermal cycling recommended for retrogaming use

facts.label: Measured
facts.value: case temperature, output voltage, ripple

children.name: UL 478 / IEC 65 listing
children.description: The brick is certified as a component, not as a consumer appliance: UL 478 'Power Supply Units' in the United States, the equivalent IEC/EN 41003 and IEC 65 (BS 415 in the UK, VDE in West Germany) in Europe, plus CSA in Canada and Singapore's NLS scheme. Getting on the list required submitting the transformer winding instruction and the critical parts list, because those are the two things that cannot be verified by testing a finished unit.

facts.label: US standard
facts.value: UL 478, Power Supply Units

facts.label: File number seen
facts.value: 13J5, moulded into the case, with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: Other marks seen
facts.value: CSA, NLS (Singapore), and on European units VDE

children.note: UL 478 was the correct standard in 1982-84; it has since been withdrawn and replaced by UL 62368-1, which moved from a shock-hazard model to a hazard-based energy model. That change is why the old test voltages and limits quoted here no longer appear in current standards.

children.name: Isolation, creepage and clearance
children.description: The physical rules that make the layout safe: a primary-to-secondary creepage of about 6.4 mm and clearance of 3.2 mm for a 250 V basic insulation, the earthed foil between the windings, and the bobbin and terminal block designed so that a wire cannot fall across the isolation barrier. Every one of those dimensions is on the drawing and is checked at the follow-up inspection.

facts.label: Pinhole test
facts.value: a 0.5-1.0 mm hole in the earth screen is allowed to be probed without breakdown

children.note: Exact creepage and clearance figures depend on the pollution degree, the insulation type and the applicable standard edition; the values above are the order of magnitude for basic insulation at these voltages, not a substitute for the standard's tables.

roots.name: Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV)
roots.description: The box on the C64 mainboard that turns the VIC-II's separate luma and colour outputs plus the SID's audio into one RF carrier for a television's antenna socket. Commodore published it as schematic 251025 and 251696: a handful of Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, one trimmer capacitor and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack and a ten-way terminal strip on the edge of the board.

facts.label: US channel 3 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 61.25 MHz, chroma 64.25 MHz, sound 67.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: US channel 4 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 67.25 MHz, chroma 70.25 MHz, sound 73.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: UK channel 36 (PAL-I, UHF)
facts.value: vision carrier 591.25 MHz, chroma 585.75 MHz, sound 585.25 MHz, intercarrier 5.5 MHz

facts.label: Channel switching
facts.value: an H-L switch (channel 3/4) on NTSC machines; a tuning dial on PAL machines

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the C64's ~9 V unregulated rail, stabilised internally by a zener

facts.label: Terminals
facts.value: 1 +B, 2 sync+luma in, 3 colour in, 4 audio in, 5 composite out, 6 sync+luma out, 7 colour out, 8 intercarrier selector, 9 RF out, 10 channel trimmer

facts.label: Size
facts.value: ~63.6 x 62.6 x 24 mm for the 251025 module

roots.note: Three corrections to the brief. First, 55.25 and 62.25 MHz do not match any broadcast allocation: neither is US channel 3 nor a UK channel. US VHF channel 3 has its picture carrier at 61.25 MHz; the European PAL C64 shipped for UK channel 36, with the vision carrier at 591.25 MHz. Second, the part numbers 474040 and 474041 could not be corroborated in any Commodore document I could reach; the documented modulator identifiers are the schematic numbers 251025 and 251696 and the part numbers 250469, 326130-01, 51A1-10 and the Mitsumi MD6 series. Third, the standard Commodore modules are discrete through-hole boards with Japanese transistors, not thin-film hybrids - the hybrid subtree is included as illustrative.

children.name: Video amplifier and clip network
children.description: Three small-signal transistors that take the VIC-II's pin 15 (sync + luminance) and pin 14 (colour), clip them with back-to-back diodes, and provide the two separate buffered outputs that go to the monitor connector as S-Video plus the summed composite that drives the RF section. Commodore called Q1-Q3 2SC1694 or equivalent; the earlier 251696 drawing uses 2SC2405.

facts.label: Q1, Q2, Q3 (251025)
facts.value: 2SC1694 or equivalent; Q4 2SC1730, Q5 2SC460, Q6 2SC2120

facts.label: Q1, Q2 (251696)
facts.value: 2SC2405 or equivalent; Q3, Q4 2SC2778; Q5 2SC2120Y

facts.label: Clamp diodes
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) or MA151K (251696), back to back on the sync tips

facts.label: Typical network
facts.value: colour in via 68 nF with 1k/33k/43k bias and a 68 ohm emitter; luma in via 2.4 nF and 180 pF with 12k, 100 ohm and 400 ohm

children.name: 2SC1694 small-signal NPN
children.description: A TO-92 epoxy-potted silicon NPN with a 100-150 V collector rating, used as a common-emitter amplifier with a collector resistor and an unbypassed emitter resistor. The 2SC-prefix parts were the standard Japanese equivalents of the 2N series, and Commodore specified them as 'or equivalent'.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92, epoxy-filled

children.note: Commodore's own parts list for the 326298 motherboard gives 2N3904 and 2N4401 with stock numbers 902658-01 and 902652-01, so the same die bins served both the mainboard and the brick; the 2SC parts came from Japanese vendors.

children.name: Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding
children.description: The die is a small epitaxial NPN on a 100 mm P-type <111> wafer, sawn with a diamond blade, die-attached with a silver-glass preform, wire-bonded with 50 um aluminium and transfer-moulded in an epoxy-filled TO-92 tool at 150-175 C.

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: 4-6 um N-type epi on a 10-20 ohm.cm P substrate

children.note: This is one of about forty such transistors in a C64; the silicon branch of this tree carries the full wafer process.

children.name: Semiconductor silicon, from quartz
children.description: Quartz (SiO2) is reduced with petroleum coke in an electric arc furnace at 1800-2000 C to 97-99% metallurgical silicon, upgraded by trichlorosilane disproportionation to 9-11N polycrystalline silicon, pulled as a Czochralski single crystal, sawn and polished. This is the shared root of every silicon device in the C64.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO at 1800-2000 C

facts.label: Wafer
facts.value: 100 mm Czochralski, 10-20 ohm.cm p-type <111>

children.name: High-purity quartz
children.description: Pegmatite and vein quartz, acid-leached and hydrothermally purified to 99.99% SiO2, is the only commercial source of semiconductor silicon. This is the leaf of the silicon branch.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% SiO2 after purification

children.name: Electric arc furnace reduction of quartz
children.description: Quartz is mixed with petroleum coke and heated to 1800-2000 C by an electric arc furnace submerged in the charge. The carbon reduces SiO2 to silicon while the arc supplies the heat; the reaction is strongly endothermic and the furnace is the single biggest electricity consumer in the whole silicon chain.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: petroleum coke, ~2000 kg per tonne of silicon

children.note: Almost all of the electricity for a 1980s semiconductor-grade silicon plant went into the arc furnaces, which is why the industry clustered next to cheap power.

children.name: Carbothermal slag
children.description: The liquid residue from the arc furnace is calcium silicate, formed because limestone is deliberately added as a flux to keep the furnace from silting up. It is ground and sold as cement or as a road aggregate; a few hundred kg of slag per tonne of silicon is the main waste stream of the process.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: CaO-SiO2, roughly 60% CaO

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~1.0-1.5 t slag per tonne of silicon

children.name: Trichlorosilane and the Siemens process
children.description: The upgrade from 99% to 11N silicon is done in a fluidised-bed Siemens reactor: hydrogen reduces trichlorosilane vapour with the deposited silicon as the seed, at 1000-1150 C, growing rods of polycrystalline silicon at a few mm per minute. Trichlorosilane itself is made by chlorinating metallurgical silicon with hydrogen chloride at 250-350 C.

facts.label: Trichlorosilane
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2 at 250-350 C

children.name: Polycrystalline silicon rod
children.description: A 100-150 mm diameter, 1-2 m long rod of 11N silicon, sawn into ~250 mm slices by an inner-diameter or wire saw. In 1982 nearly all wafers were still sawn with an abrasive ID saw and then lapped, which is why wafers were 200-300 um thick before polishing took them to 250-300 um; the wafer laser was commercial but not universal.

facts.label: Wafer thickness
facts.value: ~250-300 um after polish

children.name: 1SS119 / MA151K clip diodes
children.description: Small-signal switching diodes, typically 50 mA class in a DO-35 glass can, wired back to back across the sync input. They conduct only on the tips of the sync pulses and the colour burst, which clips the signal to the amplitude a television's AGC expects and stops the modulator over-modulating.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) / MA151K (251696) or equivalent

facts.label: Package
facts.value: DO-35 glass, 2 mm diameter

children.name: Picture carrier oscillator
children.description: A Clapp or Colpitts oscillator built around Q4 (2SC1730, a VHF transistor with an f_T above 300 MHz) and a miniature RF transformer, with a capacitive divider setting the feedback ratio. Composite video is injected into the oscillator's base network, so the video signal frequency-modulates the carrier directly: the modulation is done by varying the effective tank reactance with the video voltage, not by driving a separate modulator.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 61.25 MHz (NTSC ch 3), 67.25 MHz (NTSC ch 4), 591.25 MHz (PAL UK UHF ch 36)

facts.label: Feedback divider
facts.value: ~33.5 pF and 3.3 pF capacitors around the base

facts.label: Deviation
facts.value: +/-4.5 MHz from the carrier, i.e. +/-0.5 MHz of 5.5 MHz peak video

facts.label: Level network
facts.value: ~56 kOhm and 47 ohm series resistors with 30-51 pF capacitors

children.note: Channel setting is a resistor strapping and the channel trimmer, not a switched band. On NTSC machines an H-L switch on the rear panel changes a resistor or opens a contact in that network; on PAL machines there is a tuning dial instead, because the European sets have no fine channel selector - the dial is what makes a Commodore usable on a European television at all.

children.name: 2SC1730 / 2SC2778 VHF transistor
children.description: A VHF small-signal NPN in TO-92, chosen because its unity-gain bandwidth is several times the 60 MHz operating frequency so the oscillator starts easily and stays linear, and because its output capacitance is low enough not to detune the tank.

facts.label: f_T
facts.value: ~250-350 MHz class

children.note: Both are Japanese VHF small-signal types with f_T in the low hundreds of MHz; I did not verify the exact figures against a 1982 data book.

children.name: Channel and region switching
children.description: Three different ways of reaching the right channel appear across the revisions. The US 5-pin and 8-pin machines use a two-position H-L switch on the rear panel wired to change a component value in the oscillator tank or level network. Some later units bring a variable capacitor or a trimmer out to a dial so the user can tune to their local station. PAL machines use the UHF band, so their oscillator runs at several times the frequency of the NTSC one and the tank and output matching are different parts entirely.

facts.label: NTSC H-L switch
facts.value: switches between 61.25 and 67.25 MHz

facts.label: PAL dial
facts.value: continuous tuning around 591.25 MHz (UK channel 36)

facts.label: Implication
facts.value: one modulator part number could not serve both markets, which is why the service manual lists several

children.note: The C64 Wiki notes that beside the RF jack you often see an H-L switch for channels 3 and 4 (NTSC only) or a control dial for adjusting the oscillator frequency - the two mechanisms correspond to the two markets.

children.name: UHF output stage for the PAL version
children.description: At 591 MHz a single transistor oscillator cannot drive a 75 ohm television input through a long lead, so the PAL modulators add a small tuned output stage and, in the later units, an output amplifier with its own bias network. The extra gain is what makes a PAL C64 usable on a European television without a booster.

facts.label: Gain
facts.value: a few dB of tuned amplification after the oscillator

facts.label: Matching
facts.value: tapped output coil plus a series blocking capacitor into the phono socket

children.note: I could not find a schematic for the PAL variant, so the topology here is inferred from the service manual's description of the PAL modules and from the general practice of UHF modulators of the period.

children.name: Oscillator coil and RF transformer
children.description: A very small ferrite- or powdered-iron-cored coil wound on a 2-3 mm former with a tap, or a miniature two-winding transformer. The tapped winding gives both the feedback tap and an output tap, and the whole assembly sits within a few millimetres of the board's ground plane to keep the stray capacitance stable.

facts.label: Inductance
facts.value: ~1-2 uH class for a 60 MHz tank, loaded by the divider

facts.label: Core
facts.value: ferrite or powdered iron, 2-4 mm diameter

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.15-0.25 mm enamelled copper, 3-8 turns

children.note: These were hand-wound on a bobbin winder and checked with an inductance meter, then adjusted by squeezing or spreading the turns. At 591 MHz (the PAL UHF version) the tank inductance scales down by roughly a factor of ten and the coil is correspondingly smaller and looser, which is one reason the PAL and NTSC modulators cannot share a part number.

children.name: Radio-frequency ferrite core
children.description: Nickel-zinc ferrite or iron powder, pressed or moulded into rings, cores or rods. NiZn is preferred above about 20 MHz because its resistivity is high enough that eddy-current loss does not swamp the circuit; MnZn is a low-frequency material and is the one used in the power transformer instead.

facts.label: Permeability
facts.value: ~10-100 for the RF grades, versus ~1000-3000 for MnZn

facts.label: Useful band
facts.value: NiZn 1-200 MHz; MnZn 10-100 kHz

children.name: Channel trimmer capacitor
children.description: The channel tuning element brought out to terminal 10 of the module: a small screw-adjusted trimmer, most often a ceramic or a mica trimmer in the 1-10 pF range. It sits across the tank and is set once, at the television manufacturer's alignment step, against a sweep generator or a calibrated television signal.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: ceramic screw-trimmer or mica trimmer, radial or dip

children.note: The 251025 drawing shows two adjustable trimmers in the RF area, one of which is the channel trimmer on terminal 10 and the other in the oscillator's feedback network. Later revisions replaced them with a fixed capacitor plus a resistor strapping for channel 3 or 4, which is why the channel switch exists at all.

children.name: Multilayer ceramic capacitor
children.description: A stack of 20-50 alternating layers of barium titanate dielectric and internal nickel electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired at 1200-1350 C, then terminated in a fired-on silver or copper end-bump. This is the material of choice for small fixed RF capacitors because its self-resonance is high and its parasitics are tiny.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: BaTiO3 (Class 1, stable) or BaTiO3 plus glass (Class 2)

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1200-1350 C in a belt furnace in air

children.note: Class 2 (Z5U/Y5V) dielectric is used for high-value parts but has a strong temperature and voltage coefficient and is a poor choice for an RF decoupling or timing capacitor; the C64 mainboard used Class 2 parts in the tens-of-pF range on the video lines.

children.name: Barium titanate ceramic powder
children.description: BaTiO3 is precipitated from barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, then doped and milled to sub-micron size. Barium carbonate comes from barite reduced with coke; titanium dioxide comes from ilmenite ore or from a chloride process fed on titanium ore and coke.

facts.label: Precursors
facts.value: BaCO3 from BaSO4 + C at 1000-1200 C; TiO2 from ilmenite or rutile

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 0.2-0.5 um after milling

children.note: Barium is a heavy metal and the industry moved off barium titanate where possible through the 1980s; it remained standard for Class 1 RF and high-voltage dielectrics.

children.name: Barite ore (barytes)
children.description: A heavy white barium sulphate ore, mined chiefly as a drilling mud and as the feed for barium carbonate. This is the leaf of the barium chain.

children.name: Ilmenite and the chloride process
children.description: Titanium dioxide pigment is made either by sulphating ilmenite ore and calcining, or by chlorinating ilmenite with coke at 900 C and oxidising the TiCl4 in a flame to TiO2. Ilmenite is a beach or dune sand of FeTiO3, concentrated by gravity and magnetic separation.

facts.label: Chlorination
facts.value: FeTiO3 + 2C + 2Cl2 -> TiCl4 + Fe + 2CO at ~900 C

children.name: Ilmenite sand
children.description: A black heavy mineral sand, essentially iron titanate, worked from beach placer deposits and from massive ore bodies. Dredged, concentrated and smelted to give titanium slag or chlorinated to give TiCl4. This is the leaf of the titanium chain.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: ~52% TiO2, ~47% FeO in ideal FeTiO3

children.name: MA57 tuning varactor diode
children.description: On the earlier 251696 drawing the tuning is done by D3, an MA57: a junction varactor whose capacitance falls as the reverse bias rises. Lifting the tuning out of the tank into a varactor keeps the temperature coefficient and the stray capacitance low. Later drawings use a mechanical trimmer in the same position.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: MA57 or equivalent (251696 note 2)

facts.label: Function
facts.value: variable reactance in the oscillator tank

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: a screw trimmer capacitor on terminal 10 in the 251025 drawing

children.note: A junction varactor in a 60 MHz television modulator is unusual - most designs tune with a trimmer - so the MA57 may be a varicap used for a small frequency-modulation or level function rather than for the channel. Its exact role in the 251696 drawing could not be confirmed from the scan.

children.name: Audio intercarrier path
children.description: A separate 4.5 MHz (NTSC) or 5.5 MHz (PAL) oscillator whose amplitude is modulated by the SID's audio output, then added to the picture carrier. Terminal 8 selects between the two: Commodore's drawing notes that terminal 8 shorted to ground is PAL and open is NTSC PAL/US.

facts.label: Intercarrier
facts.value: 4.5 MHz NTSC, 5.5 MHz PAL

facts.label: Input filter
facts.value: 22 uH choke and a ~10 nF capacitor

facts.label: Audio source
facts.value: the SID's amplified audio, fed from CN5 pin 3

children.note: Television sound is transmitted as FM on a subcarrier, and the tuner recovers it by beating the subcarrier against a local oscillator at the same frequency to produce the 6.0 or 5.5 MHz difference that every television's audio detector already handles. Using the standard intercarrier is why the modulator could be so simple - the set needed no second demodulator.

children.name: FM modulator network
children.description: The audio signal is fed to the intercarrier oscillator's base through a series resistor and a coupling capacitor, so the oscillator's amplitude follows the audio envelope. A varactor or a reactance modulator would be the higher-fidelity route; amplitude modulation is cheap and adequate because the television's own FM limiter removes most of the distortion.

facts.label: Series network
facts.value: ~2.2 kOhm and a ~10 nF coupling capacitor into the oscillator base

children.note: Modulation depth is kept low enough to avoid over-modulation and the characteristic buzz of a badly limited FM signal.

children.name: SID audio amplifier transistor
children.description: On the C64 mainboard the SID's pin 27 output is amplified by Q2 before it reaches CN5 pin 3 and the modulator; the modulator's audio input then loads that amplifier. The stage is a common-emitter NPN with a bias divider and an emitter resistor, running from the CAN +5 V rail.

facts.label: Device
facts.value: 2N3904 (Commodore stock 902658-01) in the mainboard audio path

children.note: This stage lives on the mainboard rather than inside the modulator, but it is why the modulator's audio input could be a simple high-impedance network.

children.name: Intercarrier selector terminal
children.description: A single link or jumper on terminal 8 that reconfigures the intercarrier oscillator between 4.5 and 5.5 MHz. It is the PAL/NTSC configuration link for the whole module, and it is why one board could serve both markets with a single part change.

facts.label: Terminal 8
facts.value: shorted to ground = PAL (5.5 MHz); open = NTSC (4.5 MHz)

facts.label: Implementation
facts.value: a link or a switch contact in the oscillator bias network

children.name: RF output network and 75 ohm match
children.description: The picture carrier leaves the tank through a tap, is coupled out through a series capacitor, and is matched to the 75 ohm coax of the television's antenna input by a resistive network with a ferrite bead in the supply feed. Getting the match right is what stops the RF from reflecting back into the oscillator and pulling the carrier off channel as the television is tuned.

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm unbalanced

facts.label: Series match
facts.value: ~82 ohm and ~33 ohm resistors with a blocking capacitor

facts.label: Supply isolation
facts.value: a ferrite bead in the +B feed to the output stage

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: RCA phono jack, mounted on the module in the 251025 drawing

children.note: Most C64 installations put the phono jack on the rear panel of the machine and connect it to the modulator by a short coax or a twisted pair inside the case.

children.name: RCA phono socket
children.description: The US-style phono connector that carries the composite antenna signal. The centre pin is often nickel- or gold-plated brass and the outer shell is a turned brass or plated-steel barrel crimped into the body; the body is moulded in a glass-filled thermoplastic.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: brass, nickel- or gold-plated, 0.8 mm centre pin

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm characteristic

facts.label: Body
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate

children.name: Ferrite bead choke
children.description: A small ferrite bead slipped onto the +B lead at the RF output stage so the supply current cannot feed RF back into the tank. The bead's impedance rises with frequency, so it is a good choke at 60 MHz while passing DC almost untouched.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 50-500 ohm at 100 MHz, near zero at DC

facts.label: Material
facts.value: NiZn ferrite or iron powder

children.name: Modulator supply and zener stabiliser
children.description: The modulator runs from the C64's ~9 V unregulated DC rail - the same rail that feeds the cassette motor - not from the clean 5 V. Q6 (2SC2120) buffers the feed and a zener with electrolytics sets the working voltage for the analog sections.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: ~9-12 V DC from the C64's unreg 9 V rail, terminal 1 (+B)

facts.label: Zener
facts.value: ~8.2 V class (HZ-7A1 or equivalent in the 251696 drawing)

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 220 uF and 100 uF electrolytics plus a 22 nF decoupling

children.note: Adrian Black's redraw of the MD6 shows the supply clearly: 9V-IN, a series resistor into a zener and a transistor shunt with a 330 uF / 47 uF pair, producing a VCC rail for the analog sections. Modern practice would run this from the 5 V rail with a proper decoupling network; the 9 V choice keeps the RF stages away from the logic's switching noise.

children.name: 8.2 V Zener diode
children.description: A heavily doped PN junction reverse-biased into breakdown. The doping is so heavy that the depletion layer is only a few microns wide, which gives the device a very low capacitance and a fast, hard breakdown - ideal for a shunt regulator and for clamping.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: HZ-7A1 (~6.8-8.2 V) or equivalent

facts.label: Breakdown tolerance
facts.value: +/-5% for an ordinary zener

facts.label: Temperature drift
facts.value: ~+2 mV per volt of nominal per degree C

children.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2.7 V (1N4371) and 7.5 V (1N755) zeners in the cassette motor drive, so the same parts bins served the brick, the modulator and the mainboard.

children.name: Encapsulated and hybrid module variants
children.description: Some very early Commodore modulators and several third-party and Japanese-supplied variants were potted or epoxy-dipped modules rather than a bare board: the circuit is built on an alumina or ceramic substrate with deposited resistors, is trimmed and aligned, then covered in a clear or opaque epoxy that also acts as the environmental and RF seal.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 96% alumina or a hermetic ceramic; beryllia for the highest thermal conductivity

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: thin-film or thick-film deposited and laser-trimmed on the substrate

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: transparent or opaque epoxy, transfer moulded or dipped

facts.label: Leads
facts.value: gold- or nickel-plated DIP or castellated lead frame

children.note: The two Commodore schematic drawings I could read (251025 and 251696) both show a discrete through-hole board with Japanese transistors and an RCA jack, not a thin-film hybrid. The hybrid construction described here is real for RF modulator modules from Japanese games manufacturers of the same period and is included because the brief asks for it, but I could not verify that any specific Commodore part number used it. Treat this subtree as illustrative.

children.name: Alumina substrate and its ceramic processing
children.description: A thin, smooth, thermally conductive ceramic sheet. Alumina is made by calcining purified aluminium hydroxide, pressing or tape-casting it with an organic binder, sintering at 1500-1700 C, then lapping and laser-cutting the finished sheets to thickness. It is inert, dimensionally stable and easy to metallise.

facts.label: Alumina content
facts.value: 96% standard, 99.5% high-purity

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.25-1.0 mm, lapped and polished

children.name: Magnesium oxide sintering aid
children.description: A few tenths of a percent of magnesium oxide is added to 96% alumina before sintering to stop the ceramic over-shrinking and to fire it at a lower temperature, which is what makes 96% alumina affordable for a hybrid substrate.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: sintering temperature down by ~100-150 C, shrinkage reduced

children.name: Magnesite ore
children.description: A magnesium carbonate rock mined in Austria, Spain, China and India, calcined at 1400-1700 C to magnesia. In the 1980s most ceramic-grade magnesia was calcined from seawater or from brine, but the rock remains the classic source.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: MgCO3, becoming MgO above ~1400 C

children.name: Thin-film and thick-film resistor networks
children.description: A film of nickel-chromium is deposited by vacuum evaporation or sputtering onto the alumina, then patterned by photolithography and etching. Because the sheet resistance of the film is very uniform the as-deposited value is already within a few percent, so a trim brings it to its exact value.

facts.label: Thin film
facts.value: NiCr sputtered, ~50-500 ohm per square

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: sand-blast trim to 5-10% before laser trimming; laser trim to 0.1-1% became cheap only in the late 1980s

facts.label: TCR
facts.value: 25-100 ppm/K, far better than a thick-film resistor

children.note: Thick film, a screen-printed ruthenium-oxide paste fired at 800-900 C, was the normal choice for a cheap RF module in 1982; thin film was reserved for precision timing and gain stages.

children.name: Ruthenium-oxide cermet paste
children.description: The thick-film resistor material: finely divided ruthenium dioxide mixed with a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed through a 100-250 um mesh and fired on a belt furnace at 800-900 C. The glass binds conductor and semiconductor together, and the resistance is set largely by how much glass is in the paste.

facts.label: Sheet resistivity
facts.value: 10-1000 ohm per square depending on the paste

children.note: Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal and one of the rarest elements in industrial use; it is why thick-film resistors are more expensive than the carbon-film parts they replaced in value terms.

children.name: Ruthenium, from anode slime
children.description: Recovered commercially from the nickel-copper mattes of Sudbury-type nickel ores, where it concentrates in the anode slime. The slime is dissolved and the platinum-group metals separated by selective precipitation and solvent extraction.

facts.label: Abundance
facts.value: ~1 part per billion in the Earth's crust, among the rarest stable elements

children.name: Nickel matte and anode slime
children.description: Copper and nickel concentrates are smelted to a matte, converted to blister metal, then electrolytically refined in a copper or nickel tankhouse. Noble metals fall out of solution as an anode slime, which is filtered, dissolved in aqua regia and separated.

children.name: Epoxy encapsulant as RF seal
children.description: A clear or opaque filled epoxy poured or transfer moulded over the finished substrate. In RF modules it does three jobs at once: it excludes moisture and contaminants, it holds the components against vibration, and - because it is a low-loss dielectric with a stable dielectric constant - it fixes the stray capacitance around the tank, which is what stops the carrier drifting with humidity. A conductive epoxy variant is used as a ground plane on the reverse of the substrate.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight for low CTE and low moisture uptake

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~3.5-4.5, low and stable

facts.label: CTE
facts.value: 15-25 ppm/K filled, versus 50-70 unfilled

children.name: Gold-plated DIP lead frame
children.description: The substrate is attached to a lead frame by reflow or conductive epoxy, and the frame's pins are plated. Gold is used where the RF signal leaves the module, because a nickel or tin surface has poor conductivity at 60 MHz and tarnishes; in cheap modules only the signal pins are gold and the supply pins are tinned.

facts.label: Frame
facts.value: nickel-iron or copper alloy strip, stamped and formed

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel on signal pins, tin on supply pins

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: ~0.5-2 um hard gold in the 1980s

children.note: Hard gold plating came in because gold on soft gold diffused into the bond pads.

children.name: Gold and its ore
children.description: Gold is recovered by cyanide leaching of ore and tailings after gravity and flotation concentration, then adsorbed on activated carbon and electrowon or precipitated with zinc, and finally refined by electrolysis to 99.99%. This is the leaf of the gold chain.

facts.label: Refining purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) minimum for contact plating

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: pH 10-10.5 with lime and oxygen, 1-5 g cyanide per tonne of ore

children.name: Cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption
children.description: Crushed and agglomerated ore is soaked in dilute alkaline cyanide with aeration; gold dissolves as the dicyanoaurate complex and is adsorbed on activated carbon columns, stripped with hot caustic soda and zinc dust, smelted, and electrolytically refined.

facts.label: Adsorption
facts.value: ~0.5-2 g gold per tonne of carbon

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: Wohlwill electrolysis to 99.99% gold

children.name: Hybrid module assembly and transfer moulding
children.description: The die or chip components are bonded to the substrate, the lead frame is attached, and the whole assembly is transfer moulded in epoxy: a silicone-rubber mould loaded with epoxy powder is vibrated to pack it around the part, the encapsulant is pressed in, and it is cured at 150-175 C. This is the same process used for every integrated circuit in the machine.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 20-60 s per shot for a small mould

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-175 C, several minutes

children.note: For a hybrid the mould is room-temperature or low-temperature cured so that the deposited film and any surface-mounted parts survive; for an IC the epoxy is moulded at full cure temperature.

children.name: Attaching the substrate to the lead frame
children.description: The substrate is aligned to the lead frame to within a few microns, given a thin coat of conductive epoxy - silver-filled epoxy is the usual choice because it cures at only 150-200 C - or a screen-printed solder paste is printed and reflowed, then the assembly is baked so the die attaches without stress. Silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and can debond with thermal cycling, which is the classic failure mode of a hybrid module.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: 5-25 um for conductive epoxy; 1-10 um for solder attach

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-200 C for 1-4 h for silver epoxy

children.note: Solder attach gives a better thermal cycle but stresses the ceramic badly on cooling because of the CTE mismatch between alumina and a Cu-Ni lead frame; this is why high-reliability hybrids prefer a compliant attach.

children.name: Silver-filled conductive epoxy
children.description: Epoxy resin loaded with 50-80% silver flakes. The flakes touch each other to form a percolating conductor while the epoxy gives mechanical strength and cures at a temperature the chip and substrate tolerate. Bulk resistivity is about 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm, two to three orders of magnitude worse than a metal, so it is used for bonding and for conductive fill, never for signal.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 50-80 wt% silver flake, ~5-50 um flakes

children.note: Loading the epoxy with gold instead of silver gives a non-migrating adhesive used in medical and aerospace die attach, but at roughly ten times the cost.

children.name: Chip inductor and chip capacitor
children.description: In a hybrid RF module the high-value capacitors and the low-value inductors are not screen-printed but chip-bonded: a fired ceramic chip capacitor with metallised terminations is reflowed onto the substrate, and an inductor is a tiny spiral of metallised polyimide on a ceramic chip. The polyimide is photosensitised, plated, etched and diced, so the inductance is set by the artwork rather than by a winding machine.

facts.label: Chip capacitor
facts.value: fired BaTiO3 or tantalum, terminated in fired silver or a solderable metal

facts.label: Chip inductor
facts.value: photosensitised polyimide spiral on alumina, 1-100 nH typical

children.note: Chip inductors were a 1990s development for RF modules above about 100 MHz; a 60 MHz television modulator in 1982 used a wound coil, and the chip parts that were used were almost all capacitors.

children.name: Laser trimming of the film resistors
children.description: A laser is pulsed at a deposited resistor while a bridge measures its value, cutting a slot in the film a few microns wide to raise the resistance by a controlled amount. Each pulse changes the value by a known increment and the bridge closes the loop, so a resistor can be trimmed to 0.1% or better in a fraction of a second. Before laser trimming was cheap, the same slot was cut by abrading with a sand jet under a bridge, which was slower and only got to about 5%.

facts.label: Trim resolution
facts.value: ~0.01% per pulse

children.note: Laser trimming became standard in thick-film hybrid manufacture in the late 1980s; a 1982 module was trimmed by a mechanical probe that cut a slot in the film, or not trimmed at all.

children.name: Substrate alignment and RF screening
children.description: After assembly the module is screened: an RF sweep is injected at the output terminal and the response curve is checked against a mask. A damaged substrate, a lifted chip termination or a cracked lead frame shows up as a notch in the response, which is why a hybrid modulator's yield is dominated by the ceramic and the assembly rather than by the design.

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: swept-response substitution with an RF sweep generator and a detector

facts.label: Pass criterion
facts.value: within a mask on insertion loss, return loss and resonance

children.note: Screen-on-substrate testing in the bare form was a 1990s technique; a 1982 hybrid was tested only after encapsulation, so a realignment meant re-encapsulating.

children.name: Modulator part numbers and revisions
children.description: Commodore changed the modulator repeatedly and warned in the service manual that most modulators are different and the parts are not interchangeable between mainboards. Documented identifiers include 250469 (the short-board C64C), 326130-01, 51A1-10 Rev 2, and Japanese Mitsumi-built modules MD6-UE3603 for PAL and MD6-VA3402 / VA3403 / VA3405 for NTSC.

facts.value: 220 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V radial
2 x 4.7 uF 16 V radial

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-UE3603
facts.value: 470 uF 10 V, 2 x 100 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V - the PAL version

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-VA3402/3403/3405
facts.value: NTSC versions with different electrolytic sets

children.note: The part numbers 474040 and 474041 in the brief could not be found in any Commodore document or parts list I could reach. If they are real they are most likely internal drawing or vendor numbers rather than the field-replaceable part numbers listed here.

children.name: Mitsumi-built modules
children.description: Mitsumi Electric was a major Japanese supplier of consumer-electronics subassemblies and shipped RF modulator modules to Commodore. The MD6 prefix denotes the module family; the suffix distinguishes NTSC from PAL and the electrolytic set.

facts.label: PAL
facts.value: MD6-UE3603

children.name: The 1984 C64C video path
children.description: The later C64 boards do not simply carry a better modulator - they changed where the signal is encoded. A dedicated video encoder IC generates the composite and separate luma/chroma outputs from the VIC-II's signals, so the video is encoded once, to a defined standard, outside the modulator; the RF modulator is then reduced to a device that only has to put that composite onto a carrier and add the audio. The contrast with the breadbin is that there the modulator itself was the video encoder as well as the modulator.

facts.label: Encoding point
facts.value: moved off the modulator onto a dedicated encoder IC

facts.label: Result
facts.value: composite and S-Video are available regardless of whether the RF modulator is fitted

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: the RF modulator becomes a purely analogue RF carrier generator

children.note: The existence of a dedicated CMOS video encoder on the C64C is well established in the enthusiast literature and C64-Wiki has a page stub for the part, but I could not open a primary source to confirm the device marking or its function in this context. The US and PAL channel frequencies quoted above are standard broadcast allocations and are high confidence; the encoder part number is not.

children.name: Video encoder integrated circuit
children.description: A mask-programmed device that takes the VIC-II's luminance and chrominance plus the synchronisation inputs and generates composite video and separate luma and chrominance outputs internally, using on-chip resistor-string DACs for the levels. Building the encoder alongside the VIC-II was what made the S-Video output clean enough to be worth using.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: luminance/chrominance to composite and S-Video encoding, with internal level DACs

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: driven from the 14.318 MHz colour clock

children.note: I could not verify the exact part number or its manufacturer from a primary source; treat this node as a description of the function rather than of a confirmed device.

children.name: The 'toad' module nickname
children.description: Early Commodore modulators are sometimes described by hobbyists as a toad or a blob: the epoxy-covered module sits on the mainboard with its lead frame splayed out, and from the top it does look like an animal. The nickname is not a Commodore part name - it exists only in the collector community.
children.note: I could not find any published source using this nickname for the C64 modulator; it may come from a different platform. Flagged as uncertain.

children.name: Why the RF picture was poor
children.description: The modulator is not the only reason the C64's television picture was soft and cross-talk-ridden, but it removes the last chance to recover quality: the VIC-II's own composite output already mixes luminance and chroma imperfectly, the television's 6 MHz vision channel is a narrow band-pass, the sound is on a separate subcarrier that leaks, and an analogue tuner adds its own noise. Every stage is lossy and they compound.

facts.label: Vision channel width
facts.value: ~5.5 MHz for a 625-line PAL signal in a 6 or 7 MHz slot

facts.label: Composite crosstalk
facts.value: the VIC-II's chroma is not properly band-limited before being added to luminance

facts.label: Set-side limit
facts.value: the analogue tuner's noise figure and AGC dominate at low signal levels

children.note: Empirical tests comparing the original modulator with modern replacements on the same CRT found almost no visible difference, which is the strongest evidence that the modulator was not the main limit - and on S-Video, bypassing the modulator's RF stage entirely, the original's luma and chroma outputs measured slightly better than most replacements.

children.name: Two composite paths in one module
children.description: Because the module has to keep working as a monitor passthrough, it carries two paths: the luma and colour signals are buffered straight through to CN5 so a monitor still gets an unmodified signal, while a separate summed composite is what drives the RF section. This is why S-Video from a breadbin is clean while the RF picture is not - the lossy parts of the chain are only on the RF path.

facts.label: Terminals 6 and 7
facts.value: sync+luma out and colour out, buffered from the inputs

facts.label: Terminal 5
facts.value: composite out, the sum, also fed to CN5 pin 4 on the 5-pin board

children.name: NTSC and PAL variants
children.description: The earlier 5-pin mainboard mixed sync, luminance and colour into composite on the board itself and fed that to the modulator, whereas the 8-pin boards pass luma and colour separately so the modulator can also provide S-Video. That difference is why the very first modulators are simpler than the later ones, and why the service manual says most modulators are not interchangeable.

facts.label: 5-pin board (326298-01)
facts.value: composite built on the mainboard; the modulator adds audio only

facts.label: 8-pin boards (250407-04, 250425, 250441-01, 250469)
facts.value: the modulator does the mixing and also passes luma and colour to CN5

children.name: Modulator manufacture, alignment and test
children.description: A 1980s RF module was assembled by hand through a small number of components, soldered, then aligned: the channel trimmer is set against a television signal generator or a spectrum analyser, the intercarrier selector link is fitted for the market, the level network is checked on a video monitor, and the unit is burn-in tested with a television running.

facts.label: Soldering
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, wave or hand, flux residue cleaned

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: trim the channel capacitor to the exact vision carrier for the market

facts.label: Test
facts.value: modulate a known composite pattern and check picture, sound and intercarrier beat

children.note: The 1980s practice was to align each module against a television set rather than a calibrated instrument, which explains why modules from different batches did not all land on exactly the same channel and why the rear-panel trimmer dial existed.

children.name: Tin-lead solder and flux
children.description: A 60/40 tin-lead alloy melts at around 190-215 C depending on composition, which is why it was the universal electronics solder of the era; the lead keeps the melting point low and wets the copper lead frames and the nickel-plated transistor legs. The flux is rosin or an organic acid, chemically inert but hygroscopic, so it had to be washed off or it caused resistive leakage in damp climates.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: ~183-190 C eutectic, 215 C for 60/40

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: rosin (colophony) or activated organic acid

children.note: Tin-lead was abandoned in electronics from about 2000 onwards and the change cost the industry a decade of higher reflow temperatures and wetting problems; the 1982 practice was unremarkable and correct for its time.

children.name: Rosin flux from pine
children.description: Colophony, the sticky amber resin left when crude turpentine is distilled off pine resin, dissolved in isopropanol or in a blend of solvents to make the classic mild flux. It is non-corrosive but must be removed because it is hygroscopic and slightly conductive when damp.

facts.label: Abietic acid
facts.value: ~90% of rosin, melting at ~150 C

facts.label: Carrier
facts.value: isopropanol or a mixed aromatic/aliphatic solvent

children.note: Rosin was largely replaced by halide-free organic acid and no-clean fluxes in the 1990s, but a 1982 board was always hand-cleaned with isopropanol and trichloroethane.

children.name: Crude turpentine and pine resin
children.description: Distilling crude turpentine - a mixture of terpene hydrocarbons collected by tapping pine trees - leaves a viscous amber residue of rosin and pine gum. Natural rosin supply did not keep up with the 1980s electronics industry, so most flux rosin was actually tall oil rosin, a byproduct of pine kraft pulp production.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: ~60% natural gum rosin, ~40% tall oil rosin by the 1980s

roots.name: C64 mains side: cord, plug, switch, fuse
roots.description: Everything between the wall socket and the transformer primary: the three-conductor line cord and its moulded plug, the rocker switch, the line fuse, the X-rated suppression capacitor and the protective-earth bonding. The brick's case is entirely plastic, so the earth conductor never bonds to an enclosure - it terminates on the interwinding screen inside the transformer, and that is the whole of the earthing arrangement.

facts.label: Cord
facts.value: three conductors in the North American build (line, neutral, protective earth); two conductors in some markets

facts.label: Primary fuse
facts.value: reported as 120 mA or 200 mA depending on the mains voltage and build

facts.label: Thermal protection
facts.value: a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary winding, documented on the 251053-02

facts.label: Switch
facts.value: rocker or slider, in-line with the line conductor

roots.note: The reported 120 mA / 200 mA primary fuse ratings are consistent with a 15-30 W supply and the recommendation of a fuse at about 125% of the calculated input current, so they are plausible rather than confirmed from the factory documentation.

children.name: Three-conductor line cord
children.description: A flexible cord with one heavier line conductor, one neutral and a green or green-and-yellow earth conductor, exiting the case through a clamp or grommet. The sheath is PVC in the 1980s rather than the older rubber; PVC is tougher, thinner and better suited to being moulded into the case.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: stranded annealed copper in a PVC or rubber sheath

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 2.5 A / 250 V for a light-duty appliance cord

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: black or white sheath; green or green/yellow earth in the North American build

children.note: The teardown photographs show the three conductors separated inside the case and browning of the PVC right at the transformer pin, which is the classic signature of a loose or arcing mains connection.

children.name: PVC sheath compound
children.description: The sheath is not raw PVC resin but a plasticised compound: PVC resin mixed with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate or, from the mid-1970s onwards, with a polyester plasticiser as the industry moved away from phthalates. The resin itself is made by addition polymerisation of vinyl chloride.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: polyvinyl chloride, suspension-polymerised

facts.label: Plasticiser load
facts.value: 30-50 parts per hundred resin for a flexible cord sheath

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB, and a flame-retardant grade for the mains lead

children.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
children.description: Made by the oxychlorination of ethylene with oxygen and chlorine over a fluidised bed of copper(II) chloride at 180-220 C, or by the chlorination of acetylene. Vinyl chloride monomer is acutely toxic and carcinogenic, and its manufacture was one of the worst occupational hazards in the chemical industry until the 1970s-80s control campaigns.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: C2H4 + Cl2 + 1/2 O2 -> C2H3Cl + HCl, CuCl2 catalyst, 200 C

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: suspension polymerisation, ~50-70 C, 5-12 bar

children.note: The oxychlorination route invented in the late 1960s is what makes PVC cheap; the acetylene route was used where carbide acetylene was cheap.

children.name: Chlorine for oxychlorination
children.description: Chlorine is made by electrolysing a brine of sodium chloride in a membrane, mercury or diaphragm cell. The membrane cell, introduced commercially in the 1970s, has no mercury and gives much purer caustic soda as a co-product; in 1982 the older diaphragm and mercury cells were still very widely used.

facts.label: Chlor-alkali cell
facts.value: 3-4 V DC, 20-40 kA per cell

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~1.35 t Cl2 per tonne of caustic soda

children.name: Brine, from halite
children.description: Saturated sodium chloride solution, made by dissolving mined rock salt in filtered water and purging the carbonate with hydrochloric acid. Rock salt is bedded halite, mined by room-and-pillar or solution mining. This is the leaf of the sodium-chloride chain.

facts.label: Salt purity
facts.value: typically 95-98% NaCl after purification

children.name: Halite (rock salt)
children.description: Evaporite deposits of sodium chloride, mined underground by room-and-pillar or dissolved and pumped as brine. It is dug, dissolved and chlorinated, and nothing more is done to it before it becomes the chlorine that makes the C64's plastics.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: >95% NaCl

children.note: Classified under fluids rather than metals because it enters the chain as a solid mineral that is immediately dissolved into brine.

children.name: Solution mining and brine clarification
children.description: Two thirds of the world's salt is mined by dissolving the deposit in water: two wells are drilled into the salt, fresh water is injected into one and pumped from the other, and the brine is brought to the surface with the NaCl content raised to saturation by a settling stage. The insolubles are removed in settling tanks and the brine is filtered and acidified to kill the carbonate.

facts.label: Dissolution
facts.value: water at 30-60 C under pressure, several hundred litres per tonne

facts.label: Purity out
facts.value: ~98-99.5% NaCl after clarification

children.note: Solar evaporation of sea brine still supplies roughly a sixth of world salt production, but the chemical industry buys rock or brine salt because the content is far more consistent.

children.name: Salt dome geology
children.description: Salt is one of the few minerals the body actively pushes up: buried evaporite deposits flow plastically and can breach the surface as salt domes or glaciers, so the seam follows the rock rather than sitting level. That plastic flow is what makes room-and-pillar mining possible at all - the roof deforms and closes behind the workings instead of collapsing.

facts.label: Behaviour
facts.value: halite flows plastically at geological strain rates above ~1 km depth

children.name: Stranded copper conductors
children.description: Stranded rather than solid, because a cord is flexed at the strain relief and a solid conductor cracks there within a few years. Each strand is 0.15-0.20 mm bare copper wire; a 1.0 mm2 cord has roughly 30 strands.

facts.label: Strand count
facts.value: ~25-35 for a 1.0 mm2 conductor

children.name: Strain relief clamp and grommet
children.description: A nylon or rubber bushing, or a two-screw clamp on a moulded boss, that stops the conductors being pulled out of their terminals. In a safety audit this is a named inspection point: the conductors must not be able to move more than a couple of millimetres, and no strand may be able to reach a terminal screw under tension.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: a defined pull force applied to the cord, applied to all conductors together

children.name: Moulded mains plug
children.description: A two- or three-pole moulded plug permanently attached to the cord: in the North American build a polarised NEMA 1-15P with one blade rotated 180 degrees so it can only be inserted one way round; in most of Europe a CEE 7/16 Europlug with two round 4.0 mm pins. The body is a thermosetting or thermoplastic moulding with the cord entering through a separate bushing so the strain is not carried by the conductors.

facts.label: North America
facts.value: NEMA 1-15P polarised, 15 A 125 V

facts.label: Europe
facts.value: CEE 7/16 Europlug, 2.5 A 250 V

facts.label: Blades and pins
facts.value: brass, nickel-plated

children.name: Nickel-plated brass contacts
children.description: The blades are stamped from cartridge brass sheet and plated. Nickel under-plate plus a flash of nickel is the 1980s default for mains contacts because brass alone tarnishes and corrodes; silver plating was used where the contact had to carry more current or where the plug was screwed down, and silver-plated contacts remain the modern choice for high-current switchgear.

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: brass with a 2-5 um nickel or nickel strike under a 0.1-0.5 um nickel plate

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: tin, silver, or bare brass

children.note: The C64's expansion and user ports use similar nickel-plated brass contacts, and the DIN power connector on the brick uses plated brass pins.

children.name: Rocker switch
children.description: A mains switch in the line conductor, mounted in the case wall so the rocker is the only part exposed. It is a snap-action mechanism: a spring-loaded plunger forces a moving contact against a fixed one with a definite wiping motion as it passes through centre, which both makes the circuit and scrapes oxide off the contact faces.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 V AC for a small rocker

facts.label: Contact alloy
facts.value: silver or a silver-nickel brazed contact on a brass carrier

facts.label: Endurance
facts.value: ~10,000 operations typical for a 1980s rocker

children.note: The C64's own rear-panel power switch interrupts both supplies; the brick's switch interrupts only the line conductor of its own input, and the computer's switch on the 5 V and 9 V rails does the rest.

children.name: Silver-alloy contacts and arc erosion
children.description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any metal and, unlike copper, its oxide is still conductive, so a silver contact keeps working even when it blackens. Contacts are riveted or welded to brass carriers so the spring force is set by the carrier rather than by the contact material. Every make operation evaporates a microscopic amount of metal as an arc; the contact is sized so that tens of thousands of makes erode it only slightly, and so that a failed contact fails open rather than welded shut.

facts.label: Contact material
facts.value: Ag, Ag-SnO2 or Ag-Ni, on a brass or phosphor-bronze carrier

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: ~1-3 N, giving a low and stable contact resistance

facts.label: Erosion rate
facts.value: ~0.01-0.1 mm per 10,000 operations in the worst case

children.note: Modern low-voltage switches often use silver-tin-oxide rather than pure silver because it does not weld; for a 250 V AC mains switch the plain silver contact remained standard well into the 1990s.

children.name: Copper and silver ores
children.description: The moving and fixed blades are brass or phosphor bronze (copper with tin), and the contact faces are silver. Copper comes from sulphide concentrate and silver from argentiferous lead ores or from cyanide leaching of low-grade residues.

facts.label: Phosphor bronze
facts.value: ~90% Cu with 4-10% Sn, the standard spring carrier alloy

children.name: Silver refining from lead residues
children.description: Argentiferous lead concentrates are roasted and smelted, and the silver reports to the lead bullion, from which it is recovered by Parkes' process: the bullion is cooled so copper crystallises out and is skimmed, then zinc is added, which scavenges the silver and gold into a zinc crust that is skimmed off and distilled. The crude silver is cupelled and electrolytically refined to 99.9% or better.

facts.label: Parkes process
facts.value: zinc added at 1-2% of the bullion mass, crust skimmed at 600-700 C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: Moebius or Balbach-Thum electrolysis, silver nitrate electrolyte

children.note: Silver for electrical contacts has always been by-product metal, so its price is set by the lead and zinc smelters rather than by silver mines; most of the 1982 supply came from Mexico, Peru and the Soviet bloc.

children.name: Cupellation
children.description: An ancient refining step that survives into the 1980s for precious metals: the metal is melted with a lead oxide flux and blown with air, which oxidises the lead and the base metals to litharge that floats off, while the silver and gold stay as metal. Agricola described it in the 16th century and it is still the standard way to remove base metal from silver dross.

facts.label: Litharge
facts.value: PbO, the oxidised lead, absorbed into the bone ash cupel

children.name: Rocker actuator and case
children.description: The external rocker is moulded in a glass-filled thermoset or a self-extinguishing thermoplastic and clips over a phenolic or nylon body carrying the fixed contacts. The case must be rated for the insulation class and have the flammability rating appropriate to an appliance, and the actuator must not be able to be jammed in the on position.

facts.label: Case material
facts.value: phenolic or nylon 66, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Creepage
facts.value: ~4 mm between line and neutral terminals, set by the moulding

children.name: Glass-reinforced switch body
children.description: Glass fibre is added to the switch body at 20-30% by weight and the compound is compression moulded. The glass reduces creepage and raises the distortion temperature, which is what keeps the moulding from softening near a hot transformer.

facts.label: Glass content
facts.value: 20-30% by weight, chopped 3-6 mm strands

facts.label: Distortion temperature
facts.value: ~150-200 C for a glass-filled phenolic

children.note: Glass reinforcement also makes the material abrasive, so a switch mechanism with glass-filled tracks must be designed so the moving contacts never ride on a glass-filled surface.

children.name: Primary fuse and thermal fuse
children.description: Two serial protections on the mains side. The primary fuse is a small cartridge type rated at roughly 120 mA (115 V) or 200 mA (230 V), sized at about 125% of the running input current so the transformer draws its inrush without nuisance failure. The second, documented in the 251053-02, is a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary: a fusible alloy element that opens irreversibly if the transformer overheats.

facts.label: Primary fuse rating
facts.value: reported 120 mA / 200 mA, depending on build and mains voltage

facts.label: Secondary fuses
facts.value: 3 A in the 9 V AC conductor, 5 A slow-blow in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

facts.label: Thermal fuse
facts.value: in series with one end of the primary winding on the 251053-02

children.note: The 3 A fuse in the 9 V AC conductor exists so a short on the output cable cannot damage the transformer before the brick is ever plugged into a C64; the 5 A slow fuse in the rectifier conductor is sized for the charging surge of the 4700 uF reservoir capacitor.

children.name: Glass cartridge fuse
children.description: A fuse element of pure tin or a tin alloy, historically a lead-antimony or tin-lead alloy, held between two metal end caps inside a glass tube. The glass is there so a failure is visible: the element melts, an arc forms, the tube fills with metal vapour and the arc is quenched as the pressure collapses, and the tube blackens.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: tin or tin-lead alloy, ~0.1-0.5 mm

facts.label: Voltage rating
facts.value: 250 V for the sizes used here

facts.label: Breaking capacity
facts.value: ~35-100 A for a small cartridge fuse

children.name: Soda-lime tube glass
children.description: The fuse tube is a drawn borosilicate or soda-lime glass tube, chosen because it is dimensionally stable, easy to seal and does not outgas. Glass tubing is made by melting the batch and drawing the softened gather between rollers, so the wall thickness and diameter stay within a few microns along the length.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 70-74% SiO2, ~13% Na2O, ~10% CaO, with alumina and magnesia

children.name: Glass batch and silica sand
children.description: The batch is a few hundred kilograms of silica sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C. The silica sand, dug from high-silica deposits, is the leaf of the glass chain.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: ~70% silica sand, ~15% soda ash, ~10% limestone, ~5% cullet

children.name: Regenerative furnace and cowper
children.description: A glass furnace cannot simply burn gas, because glassmelting needs far more heat than combustion can deliver at that temperature. The answer is regeneration: a Cowper regenerator beside the furnace stores the heat of the exhaust in a refractory mass, then blows the air through it on the next firing. The two 1980s designs were the regenerative box furnace and the unit-regenerator furnace.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: natural gas or oil, preheated to 600-1000 C by the regenerator

facts.label: Waste-heat recovery
facts.value: ~20-40% of the fuel energy returned to the air blast

children.name: Refractory lining and checker plates
children.description: The furnace and regenerator are lined with refractory brick, and the regenerator's internal mass is a stack of checker plates of silica or chrome-magnesite. Refractory brick is made by pressing or hand-moulding a graded mineral aggregate with a clay binder and firing it in a tunnel or car kiln; the grading, not the chemistry, is what gives a lining its thermal-shock resistance.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1400-1500 C for silica brick; 1600-1750 C for magnesia

facts.label: Silica brick
facts.value: ~94-98% SiO2, use limited to about 1500 C

facts.label: Magnesia brick
facts.value: 85-95% MgO, used to ~1700 C

children.note: Beryllium oxide had even higher conductivity but was withdrawn from general use in the 1980s because of its toxicity.

children.name: Ceramic wirewound fuse
children.description: A slow-acting fuse for the high inrush of the reservoir capacitor: a length of resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin, shunted by a strip of fusible alloy that runs beside it. The strip carries the current normally; the winding heats up when the fuse is overloaded and melts the strip, so the fuse tolerates a brief surge that would blow a straight element.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: resistance wire in parallel with a fusible alloy strip

facts.label: Characteristic
facts.value: time-delay (slow-blow); identified in the teardown by a small spiral inside the cartridge

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 A 250 V in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

children.note: The distinction between the two secondary fuses was made by inspection: the fast-acting one is a straight piece of fusible wire while the slow one contains a visible spiral or spring.

children.name: Thermal fuse
children.description: A one-shot temperature fuse: a fusible alloy link, often a fine wire of a low-melting alloy such as a bismuth-lead-tin-indium eutectic, bonded to the transformer or mounted in thermal contact with it. At its trip temperature - typically 100-130 C - the link melts and opens the circuit permanently. It cannot be reset, which is intentional: the fault that overheated the transformer is not allowed to be repeated.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~100-130 C typical

facts.label: Fusible alloy
facts.value: a low-melting eutectic, melting at a controlled temperature

facts.label: Fuse alloy
facts.value: often a small helical coil to make the melt more sensitive to a temperature ramp

children.note: The 13-83 teardown explicitly shows a thermal fuse between one end of the primary winding and the other line-in terminal.

children.name: Low-melting fusible alloy
children.description: An eutectic or near-eutectic mixture chosen so that it melts sharply at one temperature. A common mains fuse alloy is 50% tin, 50% lead melting at 180 C; a common thermal-fuse alloy is a bismuth-lead-tin-indium low-melting eutectic below 100 C. The alloy is cast or extruded into a strip or wire in air, then plated to keep it from oxidising.

facts.label: Example
facts.value: 50Sn/50Pb melts at 183 C; Bi-Pb-Sn-In systems melt at 70-120 C

facts.label: Sensitivity
facts.value: a thin section melts at a lower power because its surface-to-volume ratio is high

children.name: Bismuth and its ore
children.description: Bismuth is recovered commercially as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from anode slimes and from the residues of the Wohlwill process, and as a minor component of some tin and tungsten ores. Native bismuth and bismuthinite occur too, but refinery by-product is the industrial source.

facts.label: Content
facts.value: typically 0.01-0.1% of refinery residues

children.name: X-rated line filter capacitor
children.description: A small polypropylene film capacitor connected across line and neutral to shunt radio-frequency noise that the switching action of the rectifier diodes and the regulator would otherwise inject back onto the supply. It is rated X - that is, for use between line and neutral - which in 1980s practice meant a recognised 250 V AC across-the-line capacitor with a defined failure mode.

facts.label: Voltage class
facts.value: X2 (rated for line-to-neutral) or X1

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: metallised polypropylene or metallised polyester

facts.label: Safety approval
facts.value: VDE, UL and CSA component recognition; the mark is printed on the body

children.note: I could not confirm from a teardown photograph that a specific Commodore brick contains an X2 capacitor, although they are a standard fit in any listed appliance of this era and enthusiasts repairing original bricks commonly replace an RIFA suppression capacitor. The node is here because the brief asks for it and because the physics of the circuit requires it, but its presence in this specific assembly is inferred rather than documented.

children.name: Metallised polypropylene film capacitor
children.description: A 6-12 um polypropylene film is metallised with vapour-deposited aluminium to form the electrodes, then wound with a polypropylene or paper separator. Because the metallisation is only 20-50 nm thick it self-heals when a dielectric breakdown occurs: the arc evaporates the local metal, the arc is extinguished, and the damaged area is electrically isolated.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: polypropylene or polyester, ~6-12 um

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vapour-deposited aluminium, ~20-50 nm

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: clears a dielectric fault by evaporating the electrode around it

children.note: Self-healing metallised film is why these capacitors are chosen for snubber and suppression duty: a transient across the line does not destroy the part.

children.name: Polypropylene film
children.description: Made by polymerising propylene from a steam cracker in a slurry or gas-phase process; the resulting isotactic polypropylene is extruded into a thin film, biaxially oriented for tear strength, and wound onto a core. It is the normal dielectric for a suppression capacitor because it does not soften or shrink with temperature the way polyester does.

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: propylene from the steam cracker

children.name: Propylene from natural gas liquids
children.description: Propane is separated from natural gas liquids or from a crude fraction, mixed with butane, and steam cracked at 800-900 C in coils of 304H stainless steel with a residence time under a second. The cracked gas is quenched, compressed, hydrogenated to remove acetylenes, and the propylene is separated by distillation. This is the same propylene that goes into the C64's plastics.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: propylene and mixed butenes

children.name: Naphtha fraction
children.description: A refinery streams a barrel of crude into fractions by boiling point; naphtha is everything from roughly 30 to 200 C - light naphtha, heavy naphtha and kerosine - and it is the feed for the steam cracker. In 1982 a large integrated cracker was built next to the refinery so the hot naphtha could be piped straight across.

facts.label: Cut
facts.value: ~30-200 C boiling range

facts.label: Typical feed
facts.value: light naphtha, C6-C9 paraffins

children.note: The cracker does not need a specific molecule: anything in the naphtha range at sufficient severity will crack. That is why the plastics industry sits downstream of the refinery in a way the electronics industry does not.

children.name: Crude distillation tower
children.description: A fractionating tower 30-50 m tall, internally a stack of trays, separates a barrel of crude continuously by boiling point: residue at the bottom, then gas oil, diesel, kerosine, naphtha, and finally overhead gases. It runs at essentially atmospheric pressure with steam stripping at the top.

facts.label: Trays
facts.value: 20-40 bell or valve trays in a 1980s unit

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 GJ of fuel per barrel of crude distilled

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The raw petroleum lifted from a wellhead and separated from its associated gas and water. A barrel is 42 US gallons of a hydrocarbon mixture whose composition depends entirely on where it came from - the same crude ranges from light paraffinic to heavy asphaltic. This is the leaf of the petroleum branch and, for the C64, the origin of nearly every polymer and every solvent in the machine.

facts.label: Specific gravity
facts.value: 0.8-1.0, light to heavy

facts.label: Sulfur
facts.value: 0.05-4% by weight

children.note: The case's ABS, the capacitor's polypropylene and polyester films, the epoxy's phenolic and amine hardeners, the cord's PVC and the switch's thermoset all trace back to barrels of this.

children.name: Film winding and vacuum metallisation
children.description: The film web is wound on a rotating vacuum-chamber drum while a wire feed head traverses it, laying down an aluminium layer 20-50 nm thick by resistive evaporation. At the same time a nucleation solution is dosed in to promote columnar crystal growth, so the metal grains follow the drum direction and the resulting capacitor has a low-loss, self-healing electrode. The web is slit to width and the capacitor is wound from slits onto a core.

facts.label: Evaporation rate
facts.value: ~1-3 nm per second, drum 300-800 mm diameter

facts.label: Slit width
facts.value: 5-30 mm for small parts

children.note: The un-metallised capacitor film is made on a separate line by a similar drum winder with a die and a chill roll; the metallising line normally sits downstream of the film line in the same plant.

children.name: Cast film production
