children.description: Polypropylene is extruded through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll, then stretched and heat-set so it is strong in both directions, then slit into webs 20-60 um wide. A plain film is wound on the same type of machine as the metallised film, so the two steps are usually separate plants.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: machine-direction orientation is typical for capacitor film

children.name: RIFA suppression capacitors
children.description: RIFA, a Swedish manufacturer of interference-suppression components, became in the 1980s the dominant supplier of X-rated capacitors across Europe, and its part numbers are still legible in equipment of that vintage. Decades later their products became notorious: the electrolyte in the metallised film absorbed moisture, the capacitor began to draw a leakage current, heat up, and in the worst cases short and catch fire in equipment that had been sitting unused for years. The whole class of parts is now treated as a safety hazard and is routinely replaced on sight.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: metallised polypropylene, X2 rated, typically 0.01-0.68 uF

facts.label: Supply chain
facts.value: dominant European supplier of X capacitors in the 1980s

children.note: The failure was a design weakness rather than a manufacturing defect: the parts used a metallised film and a construction that did not resist humidity ingress, and decades-old parts can now be unsafe even without having been used hard. This is one of the few places where a component from 1984 is a present-day fire risk.

children.name: Protective earth bonding
children.description: The brick is entirely moulded ABS with no metal chassis, so there is nothing external to bond earth to. The earth conductor runs from the plug, into the epoxy-filled case, and terminates on the aluminium or copper screen buried between the transformer's primary and secondary windings. The earthing path therefore closes and opens entirely inside one potted block, and the C64 itself has an unconnected earth: the supply behaves like a Class II appliance even though it carries an earth conductor.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: all-plastic ABS, no metal enclosure

facts.label: Bond point
facts.value: the interwinding screen inside the transformer

facts.label: Continuity test
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded screen

children.note: A two-conductor cord with no earth at all would have been perfectly acceptable for a doubly-insulated Class II appliance of this size, and some Commodore builds do use a two-wire cord. Carrying an earth into an all-plastic supply is belt-and-braces: it protects against the earth pin being energised by a primary-secondary fault inside the transformer, which is precisely what the interwinding screen does.

children.name: Interwinding screen foil
children.description: A thin aluminium or copper foil wrapped between the primary and the secondary windings, with the earth conductor crimped to a tab on it. Its purpose is to intercept capacitive current that would otherwise couple the hazardous primary voltage onto the secondary; the foil is deliberately not bonded to either winding, so it must be insulated from both and must survive a probe voltage without puncturing.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: aluminium or copper foil, 0.02-0.05 mm

facts.label: Bonding
facts.value: a crimp ring to the earth conductor, not soldered to either winding

children.note: In an all-plastic supply the screen is the only thing the earth conductor is bonded to, so this crimp is a single point of failure for the earth path and a named inspection point in the safety audit.

children.name: Safety approvals and standards
children.description: The brick is certified as a component rather than as an appliance. In the United States that is UL 478, Power Supply Units, with the file number moulded into the case - 13J5 with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER' on the 3-83 build. In Canada it is CSA, in Singapore the NLS scheme, and in West Germany VDE. Each is a recognised component mark; the finished C64 was then certified separately under whichever national scheme applied to the appliance.

facts.label: US
facts.value: UL 478, file 13J5

facts.label: Canada
facts.value: CSA

facts.label: Singapore
facts.value: NLS

facts.label: Europe
facts.value: VDE; the appliance-level standard was IEC 65 / BS 415 / EN 41003

children.note: UL 478 was the correct US standard in 1982-84 and has since been withdrawn in favour of UL 62368-1, which replaced the shock-hazard model with a hazard-based energy model; the test voltages and limits quoted in this tree are the 1980s values and will not appear in the current standard.

children.name: The safety file
children.description: Listing is not just a test. The applicant submits a design file: schematic, printed-board artwork, bill of materials, critical-components list, the transformer's winding instruction and insulation system drawing, the enclosure material specifications, and the test report. The follow-up inspection checks that production still matches the file, and it is the reason a safe transformer cannot simply be substituted with a cheaper one after manufacture.

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: the transformer, the line capacitor, the switch, the fuse holder, the cord set and the enclosure flammability

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: periodic factory inspection of the listed factory

children.note: Every listed appliance of the era had a manual, a technical file and a quality plan, and the follow-up inspection was where most of the safety effort actually happened - the type test is the easy part.

children.name: Routine production tests
children.description: Beyond the type tests, every unit gets a dielectric withstand test between the primary and the secondaries, an earth-continuity test, and a functional test with a load on both outputs. The dielectric withstand is the test that actually keeps people alive, because the failure it detects - a foil short, a pinched wire, a solder splash across the bobbin - is the fault that puts mains on a 5 V rail.

facts.label: Dielectric withstand
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for about 1 s, leakage current monitored

facts.label: Functional
facts.value: both outputs loaded and measured, case temperature observed

children.name: Lot sampling and the critical-component control plan
children.description: Listing does not mean every unit is tested at every test. Instead the manufacturer submits a control plan: the dielectric withstand and earth continuity are 100% tests because they are the safety-critical ones, while the routine functional and leakage-current checks are sampled at an agreed quality level - typically one in three to one in thirty, with any failure escalating the lot to 100%. Critical components (the transformer, the switch, the fuse, the line capacitor, the cord set) come only from named manufacturers and are subject to incoming inspection.

facts.label: Safety tests
facts.value: 100% dielectric withstand, 100% earth continuity

facts.label: Functional tests
facts.value: sampled, typically AQL 2.5 or 6.5

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: from a named-vendor list only, with certificate-of-conformance required

children.note: This division of labour is why a cheap 1980s appliance could be certified at all: the safety-relevant parameters were checked on every unit and everything else was sampled.

children.name: Lot definition and rejection
children.description: A lot is normally one shift's or one day's production from one set of tools. When a sampled test fails, the whole lot is quarantined, 100% tested, and the failing unit traced back to a component lot; if the failure rate exceeds the reject number the lot is rejected and the process capability reviewed. This is the mechanism that turns a bad batch of glass into a recall rather than a field failure.

facts.label: Lot size
facts.value: typically one shift, one line, one component lot

facts.label: Reject number
facts.value: from the original sample plan, not re-derived
